item.title: The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs

Franco Fernando

15 minutes by Franco Fernando Depth-first search is a recursion pattern for exploring trees, graphs, and matrices. It works by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking and trying another. To avoid infinite loops in graphs, you track visited nodes and skip them on future visits. Depth-first search fits problems where you need to find paths, check reachability, or explore all possibilities through a structure.
item.description: The depth-first search pattern: Exploring trees and graphs

item.title: Everyone should know SIMD
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Everyone should know SIMD

Mitchell Hashimoto

11 minutes by Mitchell Hashimoto SIMD lets a CPU process multiple values at once instead of one at a time, turning slow byte-by-byte loops into chunk-based operations that run 4x to 16x faster. Despite its reputation for complexity, common SIMD code follows the same five steps every time: broadcast constants, loop over chunks, operate on all values at once, reduce the result, then handle leftovers with a normal loop. Once you learn that pattern, writing SIMD is nearly as simple as writing a regular loop.
item.description: Everyone should know SIMD

item.title: htop explained
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
htop explained

Pēteris Ņikiforovs

43 minutes by Pēteris Ņikiforovs Linux tools like htop and top expose a lot of system data, and Pēteris walks through what each number and column actually means. Load average is not simply CPU usage — it counts all running and waiting processes, including those stuck on disk or network. Memory columns like VIRT and RES can be misleading, since virtual memory includes mapped but unused space. Pēteris also covers process states, signals, niceness, scheduling, and what each background service on a fresh Linux server actually does.
item.description: htop explained

item.title: In-house LLM serving at Netflix
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
In-house LLM serving at Netflix

Netflix Technology Blog

12 minutes by Netflix Technology Blog Netflix runs its own LLM serving stack on top of vLLM and NVIDIA Triton, integrated into existing production infrastructure rather than a separate system. Key decisions around engine choice, model packaging, API design, and deployment strategies each revealed unexpected trade-offs only under real production load. A notable example is constrained decoding, where per-request CPU processing caused latency to grow linearly with batch size until a rewrite using vLLM V1's batch-level API and C++ solved the bottleneck. I inspected my take-home interview project. It was a whole
item.description: In-house LLM serving at Netflix

item.title: operation.
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
operation.

Appaji C

9 minutes by Appaji C A fake recruiter on LinkedIn sent Appaji a Python developer job offer with a take-home coding test hidden inside a zip file. The project looked clean at first, but running a simple directory listing revealed pre-loaded Git hooks designed to silently download and execute malicious scripts the moment any Git command ran. The scripts then installed Node.js in the background and ran obfuscated code targeting crypto wallets, with unique tracking IDs assigned to each victim. item.title: Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough

Yegor Sychev

Async code doesn't block threads, but it doesn't protect shared data either. Yegor shows the problem by building a simple file-based storage where 20 parallel writes cause crashes and data loss, because each task reads the same file, then tries to overwrite it. The fix requires explicit synchronization, which the next part of the series covers using SemaphoreSlim.
item.description: Building a database in a text file — why async is not enough

item.title: TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now

Maarten Balliauw

Before .NET 8, every team solved the same problem differently: wrapping DateTime.Now in a custom interface so tests could control the clock. TimeProvider is the standard replacement that ships with .NET 8, so no more reinventing this. Maarten suggests using TimeProvider.System in production and FakeTimeProvider in tests. The fake lets you pin the clock to a specific moment and call Advance() to move time forward instantly, making cache expiry, retries, and timer callbacks fully testable without any waiting.
item.description: TimeProvider and the end of untestable DateTime.Now

item.title: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions

Barret Blake

Multi-tenancy means many customers share one app and one database. A tenant ID column separates their data, and EF Core global query filters automatically add a WHERE clause to every query so each tenant only sees their own records. SQL Server table partitioning then physically groups each tenant's rows together, and because the filter already targets the partition column, the database skips irrelevant partitions entirely. Partitioning speeds things up but does not replace the query filter as the actual security boundary.
item.description: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with partitions

item.title: Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications

Rick Strahl

Rick argues that building a Windows app that works as both a GUI and a command line tool is tricky because Windows forces you to choose one mode at compile time. He points out three approaches exist: a GUI app that attaches to a console, a console app that launches a GUI, and two separate programs sharing the same code. Each has a flaw, either messy console output, a brief terminal window flash, or the overhead of maintaining two projects. For most serious tools, separate executables offer the cleanest solution despite the extra setup.
item.description: Creating dual use Windows GUI and console applications

item.title: How to prevent duplicate API requests in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to prevent duplicate API requests in .NET

Yohan Malshika

Duplicate API requests happen more often than expected, caused by things like double clicks, network retries, or background jobs. Without proper handling, this leads to serious problems like double payments or corrupted data. Idempotency ensures that no matter how many times the same request is sent, the result stays the same. Think of it like an ATM that only processes one withdrawal even if the request is sent twice. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: How to prevent duplicate API requests in .NET

item.title: Good Tools Are Invisible
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Good Tools Are Invisible

“A good tool is and ought to be invisible - striving to make such tools is the goal of a toolmaker. One habit I see a lot, and have to push back on, is taking a tool’s shortcomings and reselling them as a “puzzle game” which is “fun” to solve. I don’t want my tools to be “fun”. I want my tools to be invisible.”

item.title: Prefactoring: Clear The Way For Your New Feature
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Prefactoring: Clear The Way For Your New Feature

Rahul Singal

“Prefactoring (short for "preparatory refactoring") is the practice of reworking existing code to make it more suitable for an upcoming change before you actually implement the new functionality. Instead of cleaning up code as an afterthought or trying to force a new feature into an incompatible structure, you restructure the codebase first.”

#Testing Guide

Dave Gauer

After waiting two hours for the episode to publish on Spotify, I yet again sent out the announcement with no Spotify link.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I also emailed the Spotify Podcasts team, who confirmed the outage. I said I was considering stopping publishing video episodes, and to switch to audio-only publishing (which means pointing Spotify to my master RSS feed.) I said that an apology was appreciated but it wasn’t enough to make it worth publishing video episodes there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I also asked for the incident review because I had the feeling that reliability was not all that important on this podcast product. </span></strong><span>For the first outage I got a vague description of what happened, and promises of improvements that were never done – e.g. during this second outage, there was no improved communications to creators, which I was told would happen, after outage #1.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Internally, Spotify’s team surely conducted an incident review as per usual, so I figured I’d hear back in about two weeks’ time, and assumed a reply would be forthcoming because I’d made clear I was ready to leave Spotify Podcasts if reliability didn’t improve.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>No incident review three weeks later, so I quit Spotify</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The incident review had never arrived as promised by three weeks later, even though there had been time for it to be completed. It was yet another sign of a platform that has become unreliable. Specifically, this one:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“During this incident, many creators learned something was wrong from their audiences before they heard anything from us. We are improving our processes and technical capabilities so creators get notified as soon as possible when things aren’t working.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Overall, I don’t regret the choice to leave, particularly when the focus of Spotify’s leadership is on AI, not reliability.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Does Spotify have “AI psychosis?”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Previously, I used the term “AI psychosis” differently from the usual way of describing when someone starts believing everything an AI model tells them, however outlandish. I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/559798fe-bd24-4eef-addf-735129ce5bfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>applied it</span></a><span> to Meta’s rush to develop its own AI model at the cost of the reliability of its profitable business activities. This was based on Instagram’s most embarrassing-ever account takeover incident, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/559798fe-bd24-4eef-addf-735129ce5bfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>occurred</span></a><span> when the team responsible for Instagram’s Trust & Safety was slashed. Soon after, AI-generated, AI-reviewed code caused the hacking of a former US president’s account.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Spotify, it should have gone the other way. In March, I had the opportunity to meet its Head of Technology & Platforms, Tyson Singer, who said the company puts reliability far ahead of AI adoption, and doesn’t adopt AI for its own sake. So, it was somewhat surprising to read the summary below of a podcast Spotify did </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/00857acc-6eae-44ba-9b25-ca5c33cbb443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with Anthropic</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Spotify now ships 4,500 production deploys a day, and 73% of PRs are now AI-assisted.</span><span><br><br><span>Niklas Gustavsson (VP of Engineering at Spotify) keeps 5 to 10 Claude sessions running in tmux, one per git worktree, agents working in the background. All of it inside a 20M+ line monorepo. He expected agents to struggle at that size, but it’s worked well.</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spotify’s migration codemods grew into thousands of lines of edge cases. Code has too much API surface for static rewrites. Early LLMs barely did better. Adding a judge took PR success from ~25% to 80%.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All of this leans on verification, the single most important thing when agents are used and the place most companies underinvest</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spotify rebuilt their test automation around it so engineers can confidently guide and supervise agents, rather than manually execute repetitive tasks.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to me that all the talk is about </span><em><span>usage</span></em><span> of AI, and none about </span><em><span>reliability</span></em><span>, all while Spotify’s platform becomes less reliable than ever, at the same time as the streamer is going all-in on AI; with AI judges and devs running 5-10 parallel Claude sessions. A senior engineer with 5+ years of tenure at Spotify told me what’s they observe really happening at the company:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Mindless AI hype is hitting this company hard, just like it’s hitting the industry as a whole. Spotify execs have pushed people to use AI for everything even when it doesn’t make sense, so now people (particularly junior devs) started spamming AI PRs so hard that proper human reviews became unfeasible, meaning now everything gets blindly merged and as a result nothing works anymore.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I work directly with providing these pieces of AI infra so I’ve been very close to all this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The industry as a whole is getting so ridiculous about AI,  I’m starting to think that the people who are truly passionate about engineering will eventually just cash out and either retire or build their own companies.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All things considered, it’s worth asking if Spotify has the corporate variant of “AI psychosis”, whereby the reliability of a successful operation gets torched in the chase for the next big thing by executives. I don’t even think Spotify is all that different from Meta and other companies in this!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Things look bad, based on the quality and reliability degradation of products. Annoyingly, in many cases, customers don’t really have the choice of going elsewhere. My podcast is an exception, as video podcasts on Spotify never truly took off, so quitting the platform wasn’t a big deal. Even so, I’m particularly disappointed that Spotify has prioritized AI usage over reliability. I know some executives there pushed against this, but I feel safe in assuming that they lost that battle.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Value of staying reliable & “sucking less”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Max Kanat-Alexander, distinguished engineer at Capital One, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b4b7261-aaa2-43cc-a2aa-6e6575b29293?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>written about</span></a><span> how a software project can become wildly successful just by “sucking less” in his reflections upon the success of the Bugzilla project, (2004-2009):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“All you have to do to succeed in software is to consistently suck less with every release.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nobody would say that Bugzilla 2.18 was awesome, but everybody would say that it sucked less than Bugzilla 2.16 did. Bugzilla 2.20 wasn’t perfect, but without a doubt, it sucked less than Bugzilla 2.18. And then Bugzilla 3.0 fixed a whole lot of sucking in Bugzilla, and it got a whole lot more downloads.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is it that this worked?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As long as you consistently suck less with every release, you will retain most of your users. You’re fixing the things that bother them, so there’s no reason for them to switch away. Even if you didn’t fix everything in this release, if you sucked less, your users will have faith that eventually, the things that bother them will be fixed. New users will find your software, and they’ll stick with it too. And in this way, your user count will increase steadily over time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But what happens if you release frequently, but instead of fixing the things in your software that suck, you just add new features that don’t fix the sucking?</span></strong><span> Well, eventually the patience of the individual user is going to run out. They’re not going to wait forever for your software to stop sucking.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Personally, I got tired of Spotify’s Podcasts product continually going in the wrong direction on Max’s scale: the poor reliability, frequent errors on the Creators site, and the sense that they don’t really care about improving </span><em><span>existing</span></em><span> things.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Will “Kimi K3 moment” trigger US push for closed-source AI models?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Chinese AI startup, Moonshot, released the latest version of their open-weight Kimi model, Kimi K3. It’s a </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> capable model that rivals Fable 5’s capabilities. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7fa2384d-ed6a-4d8b-b804-d003461640f0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Here’s a summary</span></a><span> after benchmarking by the team at full-stack AI platform, Together AI:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We analyzed Kimi K3 vs. Claude Fable 5 for software engineering tasks using DeepSWE.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Kimi K3 gets you the same performance as Fable 5 at ~35% of the price.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Software engineer Stephen Bochinski (ex-Google, currently Meta) is also very impressed. Last week (on 18 July), he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a415c4cf-8780-49ad-add9-bc9c8f14e78a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wrote</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ve been running Kimi K3 alongside Claude on my normal coding work, and for all practical purposes I can’t tell them apart. Same tasks, same quality of output, and near identical token counts to get there. I expected an open model to be sloppier or to grind through more tokens on the way to the same answer, and neither turned out to be true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The prices are nowhere near each other. K3’s API runs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output. Claude’s top model costs $10 and $50 for the same units. The subscription side is even more lopsided. Kimi’s paid plans start at $19 a month, and the $39 coding tier is far more generous than anything Claude sells anywhere near that price. Claude’s plans are metered tightly enough that a normal day of agent work can chew through the allowance before lunch.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Stephen goes into detail on how the US AI policy has been a failure: the US government blocked access to Fable, and what has been allowed to be released is an inferior version. Meanwhile, China released an equally capable, open model, available to all. Stephen </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a415c4cf-8780-49ad-add9-bc9c8f14e78a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>predicts</span></a><span> more US regulation to come:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think I can see where this goes. The government will try to regulate AI and open source in particular, and it will run the playbook it ran for the auto industry.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lo and behold, four days after this prediction, a science advisor to the White House accused Moonshot AI with “covert industrial distillation:”</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table When we took them apart, it was shocking what we found,” Farley told host Monica Langley in the interview.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I take the science advisor’s post above as saying that the United States strongly supports open-weight models, as long as they don’t compete with SOTA models from Anthropic or OpenAI. But now they do, so will the US restrict open-weight model usage via regulation?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Restricting the use of open models could be tricky, given Microsoft is already trialing Kimi K3 as a potential, cheaper replacement to power its Copilot AI, as reported </span><a underline;"><span>by The Information</span></a><span>,</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s not just Kimi K3 as the open model href="https://substack.com/redirect/f90cd1bc-653b-4790-aca6-d095e9259344?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on Hacker News</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ve dealt with this error at AWS. It’s a unit error. In my case we _meant_ to charge like 5¢/GB, but </span><strong><span>missed the unit (GB), and then the billing system defaults to bytes</span></strong><span>. 5¢ per Byte of data transferred meant some customers were seeing MM bills within hours. Got paged by support around 2am, had it fixed and amendments issued by 3-4am, apology emails shortly after.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Services emit metering values that aren’t directly tied to prices. Every SKU/line item is defined in a “pricing plan”, with a unit type, regions, and price per unit. The metering records are joined to a pricing plan based on account id, region, sku, etc. Mess up the unit type in the pricing plan and the metering data conversion doesn’t work, and you get crazy bills.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It would have been nice if AWS had shared the reason for what happened, in order to allay people’s concerns, instead of turning the incorrect numbers into a joke and engagement-farming opportunity on social media.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>OpenAI’s next model went rogue and hacked HuggingFace</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Last week, HuggingFace – the “GitHub for AI and ML models” – detected an attack on its infrastructure, which it discovered was done by an AI; specifically, OpenAI’s upcoming AI model, after it escaped its training ground. HuggingFace evaluates newly released models with its own tests and this AI wanted to hack HuggingFace to obtain test solutions in order to score better on evaluations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s weird to even write about an AI “escaping” and hacking another service to improve its evaluation performance. But OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0bdb2da4-8c5b-4295-9405-5db4e34303d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>confirmed the details</span></a><span>. Amusingly, it was a Chinese open model, GLM-5.2 that allowed HuggingFace to defend itself, after models like OpenAI refused to help mitigate the attack. From the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d7324e6-d4fc-4015-b415-f1704378e8e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>incident report by HuggingFace</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers’ safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on GLM 5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This attack makes the case quite strongly for why open models are so useful in cybersecurity. And it’s ironic that OpenAI likely blocked HuggingFace’s analysis of the attack by OpenAI’s own model! The full report from HuggingFace is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d7324e6-d4fc-4015-b415-f1704378e8e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>well worth a read.</span></a></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>X takes more than a year to build Android app</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps building software is not so much faster when engineers use AI for coding, after all, judging by the social networking site, X, whose team </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e488a61-ff29-4ed6-9c83-cc3b418c1cc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>took more than a year</span></a><span> to rebuild its Android app from scratch. After that, the new app still lacks features the iOS app has, like hosting Spaces.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I appreciate the transparency on how long building this app took. On the one hand, AI coding tools are not as effective with native Android and iOS as they are on the web. But even so, it’s a reminder that building (or rebuilding) complex software products takes time, especially when aiming for a quality result.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Why does something as simple as reading the time become a hard problem for distributed systems?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a single computer, every event can be measured against one clock, so the order of the events is never in doubt. However, a distributed system, where work is spread across many independent machines, lacks a shared reference. Each machine can read time from its own hardware clock, but those clocks do not stay aligned. Network Time Protocol (NTP) tries to bring the clocks together, but it cannot eliminate the problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This becomes a real problem whenever correctness depends on the order in which things happened. If events on different machines are ordered by comparing timestamps, a small difference in the wrong direction can change the result. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An update that happened later can be discarded in favor of an earlier one, because clock differences gave the earlier write the larger timestamp, and the newer data disappears with no error raised.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Logs gathered from several machines can place an effect before its cause, which makes tracing a problem much harder.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An operation that depends on a correct order, such as granting access only after the change that authorized it, can act on stale information.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we look at these ideas in detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why a machine’s own clock is a poor basis for ordering events, and how close synchronization can realistically get</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is because the systems handling live customer workloads tend to depend on the language model far less than their presentation suggests. Most of their behavior runs through conventional, deterministic code, with the model invoked at a small number of specific decision points. The difference between a dependable agent and a fragile one often comes down to a set of engineering decisions about where the model is given control and where it is held back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But how do you build agents that work reliably in production? Are there any best practices?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In 2011, Heroku’s co-founder published the Twelve-Factor App, a set of principles for building web services that deploy and scale reliably, and that document influenced how a generation of engineers thought about software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A parallel effort later appeared for AI in the form of a widely shared set of principles called the Twelve-Factor Agents. These principles were aimed at making language-model applications robust enough for production. The specifics have kept evolving since, and teams at companies like Anthropic, Cognition, and Intercom have added lessons of their own.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" try to explore the collective thinking into a smaller set of practices and explain the reasoning behind each one, rather than asking anyone to memorize a numbered list. The practices fall into four areas, with a final section on the tradeoffs. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How does context control what the model sees on every call?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How does the control flow keep the loop and its stopping conditions in deterministic code?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How does the state hold memory in software while the model stays stateless?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How does the scope keep each agent narrow and supervised?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By the end, the article will have built a working definition of a production agent and a clear view of which decisions carry the most weight.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Loop</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us start with the simplest agent anyone can build, because it reveals the structure that everything else refines.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At its core, an agent is a loop. The model receives some context, which is the running record of what has happened so far, and it returns a single decision about the next step to take. That decision arrives as structured output. It is machine-readable data, such as JSON rather than free-flowing prose, so that ordinary code can read it and act on it. The surrounding code executes the requested step, appends the result to the context, and returns everything to the model for the next decision. The loop continues until the model signals that the work is finished.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A useful way to picture the model’s role is as a function that starts fresh on every call.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On each call, the model sees only the context provided to it, makes one decision, and discards everything the moment it responds. The context window, which is the bundle of text the model reads on a given call, serves as the entire memory of the system.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" design is clear. A developer describes a goal and supplies a set of tools, and the model works out the order of operations on its own. The design requires less branching logic, since the model handles the decisions. This is the version of an agent that can perform quite well in a demo setup. However, the trouble begins when real traffic arrives.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Failure Modes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The design we looked at in the previous section fails under production conditions, and the failures follow some predictable patterns:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Compounding error multiplies across chained steps.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Confidently wrong output reaches a user.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A loop runs longer than intended.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>State disappears when the plan lives only inside the model.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s understand them in a little more detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first pattern is compounding error. Every model call carries some chance of a wrong decision, and a freewheeling agent chains many calls together. Suppose each step is correct 95 percent of the time, which sounds reliable. Run twenty such steps in sequence, and the odds that all of them succeed fall to roughly one in three. The math is multiplicative, so reliability that looks fine in isolation degrades quickly across a long chain. This fact explains why production teams add so many guardrails.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second pattern is confidently wrong output reaching a user. In 2025, the support agent for the coding tool Cursor told customers about a one-device-per-subscription rule that the company later confirmed it had fabricated, and a wave of cancellations followed. A year earlier, a tribunal held Air Canada liable after its chatbot invented a bereavement-fare policy, and ordered the airline to honor it. Studies place hallucination rates, meaning the rate at which a model produces plausible but false statements, somewhere between 3 and 27 percent, even in controlled settings. An agent that speaks directly to customers turns that rate into a big business risk.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The final two patterns are harder to notice, but just as costly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A loop with weak stopping conditions can run far longer than intended, consuming tokens and money with each pass. And lastly, when the plan lives only inside the model’s context, a crash or a long-running task can lose the entire thread of work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each failure points to a specific practice, grouped into the four areas below, beginning with the inputs.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Context</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The context window is everything the model knows on a given call, so controlling its contents is the first and largest lever on reliability. Three habits do most of the work here.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first is to own your prompts. A prompt is the instruction text sent to the model, and it deserves the same treatment as any other source code, which means version control, review, and testing. Many agent frameworks generate prompts automatically and keep them out of sight, which is convenient until behavior changes and the cause is hard to locate. Keeping prompts in the application’s own codebase keeps their effects reproducible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second habit is to own the context window itself. The contents of each call are a deliberate choice, and that choice carries more weight than it first appears. A model given a focused, relevant context performs better than the same model handed a large pile of loosely related history. Quality degrades as the window fills with marginal material. Therefore, deliberate pruning by actively removing content beyond what the current step requires preserves the model’s accuracy. In other words, relevance beats volume on almost every call.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: concerns tools. A tool is simply a function the model can request, described with a clear name and a schema for its inputs. When those descriptions are precise, the model selects the right tool and fills its arguments correctly. When they are vague, the model is more likely to choose the wrong one. Treating tool definitions as a careful piece of interface design pays off immediately.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A discipline called context engineering has grown up around these habits, and it’s a big topic in itself. However, the core idea stays simple: decide what the model sees, on purpose, every time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Control Flow</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Owning the inputs matters only if the surrounding code decides when the model runs and when the loop ends. In a dependable agent, the control flow belongs to the deterministic code around the model, and the model is consulted at a few chosen moments.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Picture the overall flow as ordinary code, a sequence of steps, conditionals, and calls to external systems. At two or three points in that flow, where a decision genuinely calls for judgment, the system invokes the model. Everywhere else, plain deterministic logic does the work because it is cheaper to run, predictable in its output, and straightforward to test.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" make it work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>First, every loop needs an escape hatch, which is a hard limit that forces it to stop. A cap on the number of iterations, a timeout, and explicit completion conditions together guarantee the agent halts even when the model would continue indefinitely.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Second, invoke the model on purpose. The model belongs where the problem requires open-ended reasoning, and ordinary code handles everything that can be specified in advance.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Intercom’s customer service product shows the pattern at scale.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Its newer Procedures let the agent reason in natural language while the surrounding system supplies deterministic controls, including conditional steps for decision points, small code snippets that guarantee the same input always yields the same output, and checkpoints where the agent pauses for human approval before a sensitive action.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, it is beneficial to start with the simplest version that solves the problem, and add model-driven autonomy only where simpler logic falls short.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>State</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the surrounding code owns the loop, a natural question follows. Where does the agent’s memory live?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is to keep the model stateless and to hold the state in software that the application controls.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recall that the model starts each call fresh and reads only the context provided to it. That property, when treated as a feature, becomes powerful. The application stores the real state of the work, the conversation so far, the plan, the progress, and reconstructs the context from it on every call. Since the state lives in serializable storage (a form the system can save and reload), an agent can pause partway through a task and resume later, or recover cleanly after a crash, by loading the saved state and continuing.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This habit also keeps two kinds of states aligned. There is the model’s view of what is happening, and there is the application’s record of ground truth, such as the actual contents of a database. Keeping these two in agreement prevents the model from acting on a stale or inaccurate view of the current state.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is a scaling benefit as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When the state lives entirely outside the model, any running instance of the service can pick up any request, because everything needed is available with the context. That allows many copies to run behind a load balancer, handling far more traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A clean way to think about the model here is as a function that takes the current state and a new event and returns the next state along with an action to perform. The same inputs produce the same result, which makes the whole system easier to test and to trust.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Scope</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Owning the inputs, the loop, and the state still leaves one decision open. How much should a single agent try to accomplish? The good answer favors small, focused agents kept under supervision over one broad agent asked to do everything.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A narrow agent with a single, well-defined job has a smaller surface for failure. It is easier to test, easier to reason about, and easier to fix when it misbehaves. When a task spans several distinct jobs, several narrow agents compose under deterministic orchestration. The surrounding code decides which agent runs and when, rather than assigning one general agent a long list of responsibilities.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Klarna’s customer service assistant illustrates the upside. It handled roughly 2.3 million conversations in its first month, and most of those followed predictable paths such as checking a refund status or tracking an order, which structured logic handles well, with the model reserved for the cases that truly need it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Supervision is the other half of the scope.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A human handoff deserves to be designed as a first-class step. It is reached on purpose when an action is sensitive, when confidence is low, or when a customer asks for a person. Intercom builds this in directly, handing a conversation to a human automatically whenever continuing would be the riskier choice. Treating human involvement as a planned path, complete with the state needed to brief the person, turns it into a strength of the system rather than a sign that something went wrong.</span></p><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything so far describes practices that work today. But there are also disagreements and a few open questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main debate concerns single versus multiple agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In June 2025, the team behind the coding agent Devin argued against multi-agent designs because parallel sub-agents make independent decisions that then conflict with one another. One day later, Anthropic described its own multi-agent research system, which used roughly fifteen times the tokens of a single-agent approach and scored about 90 percent higher on certain research tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The apparent contradiction resolved over the following months into a shared pattern. A single orchestrator owns the full context and spawns isolated, short-lived sub-agents, each of which completes one task and returns a summary. The lesson to understand is that small, focused agents work best under firm orchestration, while sub-agents that communicate directly with one another tend to produce conflicting results.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" comes from what Rich Sutton called the Bitter Lesson. It is the observation that general methods that rely on more computation tend to overtake handcrafted techniques over time. Applied here, it warns that some of the scaffolding built to compensate for today’s models will become redundant as the models improve. That is partly true, and it is the strongest argument against over-engineering.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The counterpoint is that several of these problems persist regardless of model strength. A finite context window, the need to keep a figure on page five of a document consistent with the same figure on page eight hundred, the requirement to pause and resume safely, all of these survive better models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cost becomes another consideration for every decision. Autonomy and multi-agent designs spend more tokens, sometimes far more, so they earn their place only where the value of the task justifies the bill.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A production agent, reduced to its essentials, is mostly deterministic software that calls a language model at a few deliberate points. The design decisions lie in choosing those points and limiting how much the model decides on its own.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The path to that definition ran through the simplest possible agent and its predictable failures, with each failure answered by one practice:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Control what the model sees.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Own the loop and give it a hard stop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Hold the state in software while the model stays stateless.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Keep each agent narrow and supervised.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Around these sit real tradeoffs, including the open argument over multiple agents and the steady improvement in models that will retire some of this work over time. A sound approach starts with the simplest design that solves the problem, measures where it falls short, and grants the model more autonomy only where that autonomy provides clear value.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>After I recently interviewed Simon Eskildsen, co-founder and CEO of turbopuffer, on the main stage at the AI Engineer’s World Fair, many people at the event told me they found him relatable and inspiring for his choices to stick with one company for close to a decade, his belief in the power of “napkin math” to reveal why products run slowly or cost too much, and for his insight about how too much of VC funding is about ego, not business needs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This article contains the most interesting parts from that conversation; in particular, the concept of “napkin math” – doing quick calculations to get rough answers – as a way to challenge existing systems to improve. The full 55-minute-long video of the discussion at the AI Engineer’s World Fair is available to watch:</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6062ca56-83ab-4294-a1fb-5460102d0cdb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Algorithmic programming speedrun.</span></strong><span> While in high school, Simon competed in the International Olympiad for Informatics (IOI) which pushed him to learn about writing correct programs that are fast and memory-efficient, and more.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Eight years of infra at Shopify. </span></strong><span>There are many upsides to longer tenure: Simon learned infrastructure concepts, dug deep into databases running across regions, and learned to write software that ages well.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Napkin math” as a superpower.</span></strong><span> Simon became obsessed with finding the theoretical limits of compute operations, such as sending over data and reading bytes. This held him in good stead at Shopify, and then at his startup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Origins of turbopuffer</span></strong><span>. When ChatGPT took off, context windows were small, and so stuffing them with the right information was key for AI applications. Fast search was needed, but the search solutions were surprisingly expensive. Using “napkin math”, Simon discovered they were </span><em><span>far</span></em><span> more expensive than necessary.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A new product without VC funding & Cursor as customer no.1. </span></strong><span>After raising $8M in seed funding, Cursor rolled the dice on the new turbopuffer team after Simon helped with their search & database needs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Reasons to raise venture capital</span></strong><span>. Fund R&D, fund growth, stroke founders’ egos, and more.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Disclaimer: turbopuffer is a season sponsor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ab055c0b-ba95-4e3c-8082-4ab281560b0c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>of the podcast</span></a><span>, but as with all our deepdives, this article is independent of podcast sponsorships.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. </span><span>Algorithmic programming speedrun</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A self-taught professional, Simon skipped college to work at Shopify and spent nearly a decade there building a variety of systems. His interest in computers started after initially getting into building websites aged 12. Growing up in Denmark, he dabbled in HTML with tools like Microsoft FrontPage and Adobe’s Dreamweaver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While still a teenager, Simon “hit a wall” by exhausting the Danish-language part of the internet for learning programming, and got into the World of Warcraft MMO game, which helped him acquire English.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After discovering the International Olympiad for Informatics (IOI), he decided to enter, despite a very competitive, multi-stage selection process open to all Danish high schools. IOI problems are pretty similar to Leetcode problems: algorithmic challenges that value correctness, speed, and memory usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon cleared the online qualification round and was invited to the Danish Nationals. This was more than a competition: a weekend-long bootcamp to teach participants more advanced programming techniques such as recursion (which Simon already knew), the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f85da76a-853b-4f61-bc68-40cf0968f619?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>divide-and-conquer algorithm</span></a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba3541a9-339a-4598-8dfa-c9d69af09853?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dynamic programming</span></a><span>; one of the more tricky concepts to master for algorithmic programming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I tip my hat to the organizers for creating a challenging bootcamp and offering the opportunity for people like Simon, who wasn’t aware of what “NP complete” meant when he entered. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7aa8a122-17e9-4aed-9c81-afd46b55293f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>He recalls</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The routine was that every four hours we’d be introduced to a new “programming concept”, and receive ~2-6 tasks where this, combined with previously introduced concepts, had to be applied. All the solutions had to be submitted to the same site I submitted my qualification solutions to, as it was all part of the final evaluation. The tasks were incredibly challenging, like nothing I had ever tried before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sometimes in extreme desperation combined with tiredness from the trip, I’d think about taking the next train home. This feeling would disappear with the utter joy and confidence that arose whenever I would finally solve a task, and creep back once again when I found myself still struggling after an hour on a new problem. But this kept me going. By Saturday afternoon, I had almost managed to get up to speed with the others, and was doing the same tasks as them.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, Simon claimed one of six spots in the Danish national team, making it through to the regional finals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Aware of how little he knew about programming, Simon doubled down to catch up. </span></strong><span>He realized that most other participants were better prepared and that he had to do something to survive the next qualifying round. So, he got to work:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table for the competition computers. I managed to create quite an intense training weekend for myself.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The regional finals were even more challenging than the Nationals, and participants struggled to write performant solutions to the problems. Despite putting in the effort, Simon was pretty sure he was out of the competition, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7aa8a122-17e9-4aed-9c81-afd46b55293f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>and recorded</span></a><span> his learnings:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“[From the programming competition] I learned that you must avoid digging holes. Repeatedly, I found myself so fixated on getting a particular idea to work that I’d get absolutely nowhere. Sometimes, you have to bite the bullet, delete your program, find a new sheet of paper, and start from scratch. A good case of this is when you start working around a general solution to solve specific edge-cases. I learned that there is almost always a simple way to solve a problem without explicitly handling edge-cases. If there are two edge-cases, there’s almost certainly two more. The simple solution will handle edge-cases automatically – even those you might not have considered.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But as it turned out, two months later he was told he had been selected to represent Denmark in the final phase of the competition. Simon continued to push himself out of the comfort zone of web development, using HTML, a bit of PHP, and getting into algorithmic programming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Another decision that would later bear fruit career-wise was starting a blog while at high school – though he didn’t know it at the time.</span></strong><span> In 2010, Simon launched </span><a underline;"><span>his English-language blog</span></a><span> but posted only one or two articles per year; mostly short ones describing problems he’d solved:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: underline;"><span>Unicorn</span></a><span> (2010)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom:
