One was about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7aa8a122-17e9-4aed-9c81-afd46b55293f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>his IOI experience and learnings</span></a><span>. The other only came about after he suffered the disaster of fatally dropping his iPhone during his final year in high school.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. </span><span>Eight years of infra at Shopify</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With his smartphone dead, Simon was forced to switch to an old-school Nokia “dumb” phone. He wrote a short article about the experience titled </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e678530b-fec9-45d4-9822-e876270ecbf6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Why I’m glad my iPhone broke</span></a><span>, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5f9c0861-53b2-42e6-a3f8-d06233c306ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>went viral on Hacker News</span></a><span>, making it to the front page of the site with many comments.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems that someone at Shopify, in Canada, read the article and others by him – including the summary of his impressive performance at the International Olympiad for Informatics – as a recruiter from Shopify flew Simon out to interview in Ottawa, Canada, where he was offered a software engineering position at the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In his new job on the infrastructure team, Simon made notes about things he didn’t understand and read up on new concepts. </span></strong><span>As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“When I started at Shopify, I was insecure about having not studied computer science and my biggest exposure to programming had been the IOI. If nothing else, preparing for the IOI taught me that you can sit down, read a paper, and figure it out if you spend enough time on it. So, I did that repeatedly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my first year at Shopify, every time I heard something I didn’t know, I noted it down on a piece of paper. Then, that evening, I would read up about it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if someone at work mentioned TCP, I assumed that surely they would know </span><em><span>exactly</span></em><span> what’s in the three-way handshake and how TLS is layered on top. And I also assumed they’d looked at Wireshark and all of that. I don’t think that’s true, but that’s what I thought at the time! So, I dug deep into everything I encountered.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Working in infrastructure meant solving interesting engineering problems at a time when Shopify was growing 120-140% in load year-on-year; Simon was exposed to problem domains like:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Ruby on Rails and databases: </span></strong><span>Shopify was already one of the world’s largest Ruby on Rails monolith applications, and working on infrastructure meant being close to the database layer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sharding and cutting over:</span></strong><span> as Simon’s manager used to say, “you cannot cache writes”, so Shopify had to move from running on a single group of machines to a shard (partitioned) setup of machines. The team did the cut-over (moving to the shard) just a week before Black Friday, the busiest time of the year.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Multi-data centers: </span></strong><span>expanding database footprint from one data center (DC) to multiple DCs</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Splitting up key services:</span></strong><span> Shopify had a 128GB machine (massive for the time) running Redis as a key-value store. Nobody dared touch it until one day the service went down. Then, the team split responsibilities up into separate services.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Simon built a framework to simulate networking conditions called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f3b59d6-3578-46f6-bd88-e28427d3ae06?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>toxiproxy</span></a><span>. </span></strong><span>The idea came to him while attempting to write a more thorough, systems-level test to see how Shopify’s application held up during partial outages. He created a matrix of Shopify’s services, and wanted to write a complete test suite for this matrix, to see if the system was resilient enough to handle some parts of the system being down. For example:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce615cac-0db8-4d6f-a8cd-3af177331f61?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wrote</span></a><span> about this problem at the time:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Having tests for the matrix was a must; otherwise we couldn’t guarantee the state of the matrix wouldn’t degrade over time. Since the tools mentioned previously require root access, we investigated proxies to simulate latency and downtime at the TCP level, but didn’t find one that suited our needs. We needed an online API to edit proxies and to support deterministic latencies, which made it suitable for integration testing.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This was the inspiration that led to toxiproxy. As Simon told me on stage:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Toxiproxy is a proxy that sits in between the application and the databases. With the proxy in place, you could do things like make an API call to the proxy, instructing it to simulate taking the database down, or making it slow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over time, we added a bunch of other ways to inject failures. With this proxy, we did not have to mock low-level drivers, but we could test failure handling really well.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Toxiproxy was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f3b59d6-3578-46f6-bd88-e28427d3ae06?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>open sourced</span></a><span> in 2014, and apparently still runs in Shopify’s CI system 12 years later, to Simon’s knowledge!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The biggest benefit of a long tenure at a company was learning to write software that ages well. </span></strong><span>Simon told me that this was the lesson that made it so worthwhile, and how often the simple solution someone put together in a week or two outlasted the big, multi-team RFC-driven solutions. That was a lesson he still uses today.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. </span><span>“Napkin math” as a superpower</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While at Shopify, Simon became interested in figuring out the theoretical limits of certain computer operations. For example, how much bandwidth does DRAM have for memory transfer? How long does a round-trip operation to AWS S3 take, and how much does it cost? What does a gigabyte of memory cost?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>He sought the actual numbers, wrote a script to collect them, and created a table with the data:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1336" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e9f44a91-3a69-4639-9ca0-be30c057110a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><span>Some of the numbers Simon measured & memorized</span><span>. See </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eff8b162-72d4-4358-8871-dbb36acdbdf1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>the full table on GitHub</span></a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Simon started to memorize key numbers with flash cards. </span></strong><span>He wanted to be able to instantly recall all important numbers. As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Napkin math was essentially just this table that I maintain on GitHub. There’s probably like 50 of these numbers and then a script that generates them all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, what does a gigabyte of memory cost? $2. What does a gigabyte of S3 cost? Two cents. What does a gigabyte of this cost? 10 cents. What does it cost on spot? What does it cost on a three-year commit? I had a massive table, then I created flashcards for almost every single cell so I know all these numbers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This was a project I started taking on at Shopify because I would review projects and these numbers would be helpful.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Napkin math enabled him to challenge design decisions based on benchmarks that had issues. </span></strong><span>As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“When reviewing a project, a product team would tell me that they chose Database A over Database B because they benchmarked both, and Database A was better. I hate benchmarks because making design decisions based on benchmarks is not a satisfying answer to me.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, you’re saying that with Database A, as per the benchmark, it takes 10 seconds to do this one thing. But it should take 10 milliseconds if you do the napkin math. Say, it’s a search query. Okay, you’re searching for three terms then. Each term has this many documents that match it. That’s this many megabytes. We intersect this many lists. You have DRAM bandwidth on multiple cores, at 100 GB/sec. So if you do the math, it should be 10 milliseconds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, now you’re telling me that the benchmark for the same thing takes 10 seconds, which means one of us is wrong! Either there’s a gap in my understanding – which is possible! – or the benchmark measures the wrong thing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Often, it would be things like the person doing the benchmark and not realizing that the query would be a distributed one, running across a hundred different nodes. And in this case, of course the p99 is going to be very high!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Simon went even deeper into “napkin math” after leaving Shopify. </span></strong><span>He </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5bbbc8ce-1f8f-497b-b64d-923a0f84fbe3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>investigated</span></a><span> whether MySQL’s maximum transactions per second is equivalent to fsyncs per second (the number of file writes per second a system can handle). He discovered that MySQL can handle more writes than the operating system could sync to the file, which was a surprise:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It takes ~3 seconds to perform 16,000 insertions, or ~5,300 insertions per second. This is 5x more than the 1,000 fsyncs per second our napkin math told us would be the theoretical maximum transactional throughput!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Typically, with napkin math we aim for being within an order of magnitude, which we are. But when I do napkin math, it usually establishes a lower bound for the system, i.e., from first-principles, how fast could this system perform in ideal circumstances?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Rarely is the system 5x faster than the napkin math says.</span></strong><span> When we identify a significant-looking gap between the real-life performance and the expected performance, I call it the “first-principle gap.” This is where curiosity sets in. It typically means there’s (1) an opportunity to improve the system, or (2) a flaw in our model of the system. In this case, only (2) makes sense, because the system is faster than we predicted.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5bbbc8ce-1f8f-497b-b64d-923a0f84fbe3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>started to investigate</span></a><span>, and learned that MySQL does grouping of transactions (not doing an fsync for every write), and it also does smart merging of multiple fsync operations that would be processed in parallel, effectively doing a “group commit” to further improve performance. This is a learning he’d later use: grouping writes together on top of S3, to reduce latency and improve cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Personally, I find it amazing how much you can learn with some measurements and by asking questions about how a system achieves results that go against what the “napkin math” suggested should be its limit!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Origins of turbopuffer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Napkin math” also played a part in the creation of turbopuffer. Simon told me that three things had to combine for the project to come to life.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Search was a difficult project at Shopify. </span></strong><span>Building search was one of Simon’s final projects at the company, and he did not have a good time with it. He used a popular database vendor but struggled to have it perform napkin math. The query plans were not exposed easily by the database, so he could not figure out what was missing and why it wasn’t performing the napkin math without reading massive amounts of source code. Also, the search infra was difficult to operate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Napkin math became a surprisingly efficient reasoning tool. </span></strong><span>As a toolkit, napkin math gave Simon a way to reason about what could be achievable with a machine, if utilized perfectly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. His friends’ startups needed fast search badly because of AI. </span></strong><span>In early 2023, Simon helped a few friends with infra at their startups, many of whom had the same problem: LLM context windows were very small (4-8 KB), and they needed to fill them with the right parts of documents, but this demanded very fast search. One startup budgeted that their new search vendor would cost $30K/month, while the existing infra bill was only $5K/month! For a bootstrapped Canadian company, the cost was too high, so they didn’t ship the AI feature.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon could not stop thinking about why search was so expensive, and why it didn’t line up with what the “napkin math” predicted the cost should be. Eventually, he laid out a basic architecture to make it fast and cheap:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Store the data to search in AWS S3</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Do some clustering and organize the files</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Get latency down. S3 is cheap and reliable, but has high latency</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Driven by curiosity about how that could work, he set out to build it. As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I just became fully obsessed that summer [of 2023] with building it. The first version was the simplest possible thing. I’m a very pragmatic person, so I didn’t get buried in detail. I barely read the literature on log-structured merge (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7752eb19-1c97-47c3-beb5-c684d3d4e008?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LSM</span></a><span>).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The simplest way to do this is to run a clustering algorithm on the vectors. You get the clusters, and then put the clusters in files. The files are called ‘cluster_01’, ‘cluster_02’, ‘cluster_03.’ Then you have a file called centroids of the clusters. Then, you search by downloading centroids, looking into them, then downloading the closest clusters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There were a few optimizations around merging clusters that were adjacent in files, just to control costs and boost performance. But this was the core of it.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What about performance? Simon:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“For the first version, I didn’t even implement a dedicated caching layer. I just put the reverse proxy (NGINX) in front of S3, and that was it! The performance improvement came from caching all of the S3 objects. It was the simplest possible layer at the NGINX level.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. A new product without VC funding & Cursor as customer no.1</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I first heard of turbopuffer last year, when I interviewed Cursor cofounder Sualeh Asif about how they built the AI coding harness. From our previously published </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf60a97e-ec6f-4622-870a-6d77d3f86989?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cursor deepdive</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The ongoing need to re-shard as usage grew became error-prone and frustrating. Sualeh told me the biggest lesson the team learned was to avoid sharding where possible in future. So, they looked for a vector database that could support multi-tenancy without requiring manual sharding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Turbopuffer was a startup that promised this, so Cursor tried it and migrated a good part of their vector search use cases over.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So, how did a billion-dollar startup come to bet on a tiny, unproven infra product with zero customers? </span></strong><span>There were a few factors:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, Cursor was not </span><em><span>yet</span></em><span> a billion-dollar company in the fall of 2023, but a relatively fresh startup. The company raised $8M in seed funding in the same month. In 2024, the company was valued at $400M, and then its valuation surged to $29.3B. It was sold to SpaceX for $60B this year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Secondly, it involved a tweet Simon posted after having had enough of building all summer, and wanting to test the waters. As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I was so sick of working on [turbopuffer]. I’d been working on this all summer and didn’t know if anyone cared. I only wanted to work on it if anyone cared. So, I decided to put it on Twitter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At that point, I had a single </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/142e54e0-b099-4c3d-8e20-bce3b125fc46?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>TMUX</span></a><span> instance running on an 8-core node somewhere in GCP. I was thinking: “if someone goes to prod, I’ll set it up properly on multiple nodes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But first, let’s see if anyone cares.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anyone who’s worked in the internals of databases would’ve had too much pride to ship anything like that; I was just releasing it like a SaaS project. Why can’t you work on a database like it’s SaaS?”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, he put out this confident-sounding tweet:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1182" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f59b676-606d-486f-83f6-7f6ad260cd0d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>The launch tweet for turbopuffer. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0e51817-a904-4289-89ae-5760c67b1626?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Simon Eskildsen</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon had the confidence to launch his product because he knew it was rock-solid and scalable:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I knew turbopuffer was reliable. It upheld its invariants. For example, you shut down all the VMs and no data is lost. All the writes are committed directly to blob storage.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Cursor reached out. </span></strong><span>The company was an eight-person team at the time, fresh from seed funding and growing fast, but with a search problem that they were looking to partner with a startup on. Simon recounts:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Knowing Cursor’s founders now, I’m sure they must have sat at the dinner table one day and were like: ‘the unit economics of what we have right now, where all the vectors are in DRAM, are not working.’</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They probably were asking why someone had not built a solution where you can put all the vectors from the codebase into S3 (to make it cheap), and move the part of the codebase used in memory (to make it fast). Then, everything sits in blob stores and you just hot load it all into cache. When you open the codebase, after a few seconds it’s all in RAM and the queries are as fast as everything else.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Aman (one of the cofounders) was already talking about using S3 as a key-value cache, which at the time, barely anyone was thinking of for unit economics.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Simon knew nothing about B2B sales at that point, and was not trying to “sell” anything to Cursor. </span></strong><span>He exchanged a few emails with the Cursor team about their use case of searching many small local codebases. He wanted to help Cursor with the unit economics, while also proving that turbopuffer works. So, he hopped on a flight from Canada to San Francisco, arrived at Cursor’s office and got down to debugging their database provider:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“When I showed up at Cursor’s office, they were having some Postgres problems. I asked, ‘do you guys have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0c9e5c2-8f9d-4d15-bfec-8560079e626d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>pganalyze</span></a><span>?’ And they didn’t, so I was like, ‘Okay, let’s get that going. Let’s look at it. “</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And the problem was the same thing as it always is with Postgres: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/823155de-00b4-485d-b577-9ea0b3fa93f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>autovacuum</span></a><span> hadn’t run enough. And so they had all of these going to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/671339ff-55fc-419e-9f2f-2f6d8d8c7cc5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>heap</span></a><span>, when they should be doing index scans, etc. So, we were talking about all of that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I was just helping them: my “database genes” just kicked in.</span></strong><span> I think this built enough trust with them to believe that if I know enough to help them with their database, maybe I also know how to build one.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was around when turbopuffer’s other cofounder, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b5e5ffd-8aef-4701-bdad-1ed68598296d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Justine Li</span></a><span>, joined that the work with Cursor kicked off. Simon describes Justine as the best engineer he ever worked with at Shopify, and together, they made more performance optimizations. Cursor migrated their local code-base search over to this brand new product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Simon promised to reduce Cursor’s bill by 95%, and delivered – thanks to napkin math! </span></strong><span>Cursor was spending around $80K/month on indexing and search; with turbopuffer in place, this dropped to $4K/month. Simon was confident about making this prediction thanks to napkin math! He did the calculations based on the fundamentals; only counting resource usage that Cursor was using, and not taking a margin for turbopuffer’s operating cost at the time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Reasons to raise venture capital</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After securing Cursor as the first customer, Simon was not convinced that turbopuffer should raise VC money. He explained his thinking:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>I understood that if you take venture capital, no matter how many smiles there are in the room, everyone’s expecting to earn a big return </span></strong><span>on some timeline that makes sense to everyone involved. And ‘everyone involved’ are pension funds in Canada.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But at the time, I did not know if turbopuffer could be a billion dollar company. It felt like a very niche kind of search engine. And that was completely fine with me!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>So, I just looked at what we invoiced and I looked at my GCP bill. And I was making this equation that:</span><br><br><span>Customer </span></span><em><span>Invoices >= GCP bill [the turbopuffer costs]</span></em><span><br><br><span>Justine and I were going to optimize the system until these numbers were roughly equal. And if we could get some other workloads over to turbopuffer, we could then start paying ourselves.</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But either way, I didn’t know if I could even go and raise a bunch of money. I didn’t have any relationships. I was an outsider who grew up in Aarhus, Denmark, and moved to Canada.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few months later, turbopuffer ended up raising a total of $700K, just to be able to hire two engineers until the end of the year on </span><em><span>real</span></em><span> salaries. Simon found that most VCs did not take them seriously for wanting to raise </span><em><span>too little money, </span></em><span>and assumed this signified a lack of ambition! Two years later, with less than $1M in initial funding raised, turbopuffer crossed $100M in annual run rate. So, there evidently was ambition!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since our conversation, Simon has reflected on the topic of VC capital and built a mental model of six reasons that justify raising external funding:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #1: Research and development. </span></strong><span>This is what turbopuffer raised for: they needed the money to hire two more engineers until the end of the year, in order to build out more of the platform. Then, they would either get more customers and generate enough revenue to not need funding, or shut down the project if it failed to gain traction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #2: Growth. </span></strong><span>When you’ve built something and want to tell the world about it, often, you have to spend money on doing that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #3: Massaging founders’ egos. </span></strong><span>Simon:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“This is a very, very popular reason! You see big numbers, you get lots of press. But I think it’s a really dangerous reason to raise money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I wish this reason was talked about more, because you are diluting all of your employees when you do it. And for some people, it can become a status game. It’s not what we are about: we’re here to build a big business together.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #4: Employee rewards. </span></strong><span>A startup is a long journey, and everyone wants to work with the best people. But there are necessarily few of these folks, so you want to reward the standout ones by raising money so that employees can sell their shares. This was why, in December 2025, turbopuffer raised a round where they let employees sell some of their equity: it meant they would not have to wait for a future financial event like an IPO.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #5: Strategic partnerships. </span></strong><span>It might be the case that raising from a VC whose network of connections is key to your business succeeding, or that taking funding from a strategic investor gives you access to their platform or services.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Reason #6: Mergers & acquisitions (M&A).</span></strong><span> Purchase another company with the funding in order to expand the business.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon encourages founders to be honest about why they raise capital funding – and to watch out if the reason is egocentric!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Watch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6062ca56-83ab-4294-a1fb-5460102d0cdb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the full interview here</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s inspiring to see how far it’s possible to get with “napkin math” and by understanding the bottom layers. </span></strong><span>It didn’t sit right with Simon to make decisions about vendors based on hastily written benchmarks that might measure the wrong thing. By understanding the constraints of data transfer latency and storage cost, he found a way to estimate the theoretical lower bounds of the system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This helped lead to more informed design decisions at Shopify, and showed him there was an opportunity to build a faster, cheaper search product than the status quo.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Getting “lucky” in business requires a lot of skill, and in-person greatly helps with first impressions. </span></strong><span>Turbopuffer’s first customer being Cursor sounds almost too good to be true. But the account from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/af14e8d4-e2a3-4867-ab2b-bcdafbef9f19?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cursor cofounder Sualeh Asif</span></a><span> – and now from Simon – reveals the ingredients in more detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Spotting a new business need: AI-native startups like Cursor saw their search bills explode, but needed search functionality to offer usable AI products</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Offering a product with a magnitude of lower pricing: what people made suddenly pay attention to turbopuffer was the promise of not “just 20-50%” cost savings, but a seemingly radical, 90%+ reduction in costs. When you’re late to enter a market (like search), you need major differentiation, then deliver on it! This is also what Cursor’s attention.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Building trust before a sale: Simon helped the Cursor team fix their existing database before discussing using his product</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In-person impressions: if Simon had not flown to San Francisco to meet the Cursor team in person, would they have taken a bet on turbopuffer?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Launching at the earliest opportunity: none of this would have happened if Simon did not announce the first version of the product when he knew it could work, but was still in a pretty unpolished state!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>It’s always helpful to be aware of the dynamic of venture funding – some of which are rarely mentioned. </span></strong><span>Simon knew investors expect returns and growth on timelines which they set. Raising money is helpful in many situations, but problems arise from egotistical reasoning, and Simon believes too many founders prioritize them – knowingly or not.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwNzkzODYxMywicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODQ2NTMxMTcsImV4cCI6MjEwMDIyOTExNywiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.JjAnfhkmaNgM7NLX8dr4oaN6YGEQeT6cM2KjpA-GziA?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. This post is public, so feel free to share and forward it.</em></p><p class="button-wrapper" In August 2025, the platform reached a peak of 45 million concurrent users. Few game engines can support that kind of demand.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Roblox itself isn’t the one making most of those games. It gives creators the tools to build them, then focuses on the infrastructure beneath them. Now, Roblox is exploring how a video world model can work alongside its game engine to make those experiences photorealistic without compromising scale or multiplayer performance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This hybrid approach offers valuable lessons for engineers building real-time systems at scale. To explore those lessons, we sat down with</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0701097-1ad7-4bd3-a4fd-63a9c7e35623?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> Anupam Singh</span></a><span>, senior vice president of engineering at Roblox, to hear from him about the world model that Roblox is using to make its multiplayer games look photorealistic, the key insights that have come from taking that approach, and the next big thing that the Roblox team is focusing on. We thank Anupam for sharing with us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, you will learn:</span></p><ul Keeping the world consistent</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keeping a world consistent takes several systems working together. The foundation is the persistent state, a running memory of where everything is and what has happened, so the world is still there when you come back to it. Then come the rules, the logic that has to resolve the same way for everyone, so the game stays fair. Physics has to be believable, so objects move, collide, and fall the way players expect. Since most games are played with other people, all of it has to stay in sync in real time, so thousands of players share one consistent world rather than thousands of slightly different ones. On top of that, the world has to react the instant a player acts. Together, this is what turns moving images into something you can actually play.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A racing game makes this concrete. The track, the scores, the penalties, how each car handles, and where every other car is all need to be exact. Every player needs to see the same thing at the same moment. If even one of these is off, players notice right away.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Reason 1: missing the systems that make a game</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first reason is that a video model does not have the systems a game runs on. Its strength, generating what looks right next without simulating every object, is also why it cannot hold a game together. It has no durable memory of the world, no consistent rules, and no reliable way to turn a player’s input into the right outcome. The simplest way to see this is to turn the camera away from something and then back. “If the character turns back, is the world still the same?” Singh says. “In most video models, it won’t be.” The model regenerates the scene and quietly changes it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: A video model can render a crowd of 500 people, but those are pixels, not 500 separate players, each with a position, an inventory, and actions of their own. Painting a crowd and simulating one are different problems. However good it looks, a standalone video world behaves more like a moving picture than a game: a guided dream, with no persistence and no real interaction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are quieter gaps too, ones that show up in how games are built rather than how they look. A pure video model is hard to test and hard to refine. With normal game code, a creator can change one rule, run it, and check the result. A model that generates the world from learned weights does not give you that kind of precise, repeatable control, which makes exacting competitive gameplay and reliable, intelligent non-player characters hard to guarantee. These are not edge cases. They are the day-to-day work of making a game good.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Reason 2: pixels are not understanding</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second reason is deeper. A video model works entirely in pixels, and pixels are not understanding. It can draw a flawless bottle without knowing it is a bottle: that it opens, that it holds water, or that it falls when you let go. As Singh puts it, pixels alone will never understand the world. Something else has to do the reasoning, working out what things are and how they behave. A model that only paints the scene has no real grip on the rules, the physics, or the cause and effect a game runs on. It is rendering the world, not modeling it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 It has no idea what a bottle does.</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A game engine is built to do exactly what the model cannot. It does not paint pixels; it tracks what exists, enforces the rules, and computes the physics. So if a video model lacks all of this, why not just build the whole game in the engine? That is the question the next section takes on.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a game engine alone isn’t enough</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A game engine is built for the parts a video model cannot do. It tracks the exact state of the world, applies rules the same way every time, and keeps that state consistent across sessions and players. Engines also compute physics directly, including collisions and the movement of objects such as a car’s position, velocity, and steering. This side of game development is mature and well understood.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">A game engine’s real job</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Photorealism is where engines struggle. To make a world look real, the engine has to render all of that detail explicitly: high resolution textures, complex lighting, and simulation for effects like light scattering through fog or the way different materials reflect it. All of that is expensive to compute, and it only gets more expensive the more realistic you push it. So engines cut corners. They bake lighting ahead of time instead of calculating it live, swap in simpler versions of objects that are far away, reuse textures, or lean on a stylized look that hides the missing detail. The tricks work, but they are also why most games still look like games, not the real world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Avoiding those shortcuts, and actually reaching photorealism, comes at a cost that falls on people, not just servers. Creators need more skill and time to build the detail, and players need more powerful devices to run it. A big studio can absorb that. A two-person team, or someone on an everyday phone, cannot. This is the real limit: an engine can give you a real game, but realistic graphics through it stay out of reach for most creators and most players. Each technology is strong exactly where the other is weak, so the obvious move is to combine them.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The core idea: a hybrid architecture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Roblox’s position is that you should not ask a video model to act as a game engine, and you should not ask a game engine to generate photorealism by itself. Instead, you build a system that splits the work so each part does what it is good at.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Roblox calls that system Roblox Reality. It has three parts: the Roblox game engine, the Roblox Cloud, and a video world model the team calls the Super Upsampler. The first two keep the world consistent. The third makes it look real.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The game engine is the part that knows what is actually there. It keeps a structured record of the world, called the data model, that lists every object and its properties: where the car is, how fast it is moving, which way it points, what it is made of. On top of that record it runs the simulation, the physics and the rules, the same way every time. Because it computes all of this exactly and repeatably, the engine can act as the single source of truth that every player’s view has to agree with.</span></p><div Keeping those sessions physically close to players is what makes fast, fair multiplayer possible, because the authoritative state lives near the people acting on it instead of on the far side of the players.</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Super Upsampler is the video world model, and its name describes the job. It does not invent the world from scratch. The engine first renders a complete but plain frame, with the right shapes, positions, and camera motion but simple textures and lighting, and the model upsamples that frame into something photorealistic. As Singh puts it, the model is mostly adding the textures and the fine detail, not deciding what is in the scene. It is a large base video model that Roblox post-trains for the task, so it already knows how the visual world looks and only has to fill in the details: the textures, the lighting, the water on a windshield, the leaves moving as a car passes. The engine does the exact, inexpensive part, and the model does only the expensive, fuzzy part, which is what makes the hybrid cheaper than either extreme.</span></p><div real.</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is a deeper idea behind this split. It is tempting to assume the goal is one giant model that learns to do everything, including the reasoning about what is happening and why. Roblox’s bet is the opposite. A world model still needs reasoning, but it does not all have to live inside the network. As Singh puts it, in a hybrid the reasoning can sit beside the model, in the engine and its rules and physics. That frees the video model to spend all of its capacity on the one thing it is best at: the pixels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Dividing the work like this only pays off if the player never feels the seam. For that, the engine and the model have to stay tightly in sync, frame by frame.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How do the engine and the model stay in sync?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The real engineering is in how these parts connect, because the model cannot be allowed to invent the world freely. Every frame, before it generates a single pixel, it is conditioned on what the engine produces. Those inputs are built by cloud systems that handle level of detail and compositing, then delivered to the edge over a content delivery network, the same way video is streamed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Take a single frame in a driving game. The engine generates a low-quality rendered frame, a depth map, the scene’s lighting and weather, and structured details for every object. Each is a different kind of signal that the upsampler will later use to render a photorealistic version of the frame.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: It tells the model which objects are present and fixed, so a car stays a car with four doors from one frame to the next. The model does not get the whole game state each frame, though, since that would be far too much to process. Instead, a retrieval step pulls only the objects relevant to what it is rendering right now. The engine stays the authority on what exists, and the model only decides how it looks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>State and pixels are also stored differently, and that difference is the center of the design. The consistent world state lives in the data model on the server, where it can be shared across every client and kept stable over a long session. The look of the world lives in the model’s video latents, which are regenerated continuously and never need to be saved. The server decides the truth that everyone shares, and the model fills in the parts that can safely differ a little from one player to the next.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The hard problems and how Roblox is approaching them</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With the architecture in place, the real work is making it run in real time, for millions of players at once. The Roblox engine and its global infrastructure are in production today. The video model side is still in the lab, not yet running in real time. Below are the four problems standing between the design and shipping the model into production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A game has to respond the moment a player acts. As Singh puts it, a player who clicks can’t be left waiting seconds for the result. Most video models can’t meet that bar. They generate a whole clip at once in an offline pass that reads in both directions across time, which can take several seconds. A playable game needs a fresh frame every few tens of milliseconds. That means closing the gap from roughly five seconds down toward about 30 milliseconds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main technique is self-forcing, the core of Roblox’s acquisition of Morpheus AI, whose founder developed the method. Self-forcing turns a slow offline model into an autoregressive one that generates frame by frame, each frame conditioned on the frames it just produced, so it can stream output continuously instead of computing a full clip in one shot.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 capability rather than build it from scratch. The acquisition of Morpheus AI, the same one behind self forcing, brought the long-context world-model work Roblox needed for exactly this. Roblox is now extending the model’s context window, so what it generated ten minutes ago still shapes what it generates now.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Multiplayer</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Multiplayer is the clearest failure of video models and the problem most specific to Roblox. A model can generate a crowd, but it cannot run one. Managing 20,000 players reacting in real time means tracking 20,000 separate states, not generating a believable picture of a crowd. The requirement is also subtle at a small scale. When one player moves an object, every other player who can see it has to see it move too. An action is not only what a player does, it is the effect of that action on everyone else’s view of the world.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" One player moves, everyone sees it.</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The engine makes this possible by acting as the server authority, computing one true state that all players share. Each player’s video model then generates that player’s own view, conditioned on the shared state, so the views differ in perspective but agree on the facts. To keep this responsive, the system also runs a quick predictive simulation on the player’s own device for immediate actions, while the server confirms the authoritative result a moment later. In the future, a player’s own avatar may be rendered locally and placed on top of the streamed video, so the movements a player cares about most feel instant. Doing all of this for thousands of players at once is an active research area, not a solved feature, and Singh describes multiplayer actions as a central focus of the team.</span></p><div class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Creator control</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A game only becomes worth playing when a creator shapes it. What makes a game fun is usually the rules and logic a creator adds, not how detailed it looks. Even a plain-looking game can take off when the gameplay underneath it is good. So the video model has to stay under the creator’s control, and giving them that control is still an open area of research.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One concrete piece comes from Lucid AI, a team that joined Roblox. Its founder built what Roblox calls a game cartridge harness, which wraps the deterministic logic of a real game engine around a video world model. The point is to let a world look generated while still behaving according to fixed, predictable rules the creator sets.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Client prediction</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The harness is also how a player’s controls reach the model. The standard movement keys, the WASD inputs, are fed in as conditioning, so pressing forward drives the generated view directly instead of only moving a character inside the engine. Taking real-time player input and turning it into the right next frame is the kind of control a standalone video model cannot handle. How creators will ultimately direct the model beyond movement, through written prompts, through the data model, or some mix of the two, is not yet decided.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Roblox’s bet: creators, compute, and a 20-year head start</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are difficult problems, and Roblox’s case for solving them rests on a few advantages. It has a large community of creators to build with and learn from. It owns its compute, running more than two dozen edge data centers and its own GPUs instead of renting capacity from cloud providers, which matters when the video model has to run for every player at low latency. It has also spent close to 20 years building the data model, the structured record of objects and physics the whole hybrid depends on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To strengthen the AI side, Roblox brought together founders from several labs and gave them autonomy under a short set of values. Respect the community, take responsibility, get stuff done. Each team came in solving a different piece of the problem. Morpheus AI brought self forcing and the low-latency, long-context work behind it. Lucid AI brought the game cartridge harness, the bridge between deterministic game logic and a video model. Dynamics Lab brought a real-time, general-domain world engine that lets a person upload any image, a photo, a drawing, a painting, and step into it as a live, interactive world they can shape with text prompts and share with friends to play instantly. Put together, those are the pieces of speed, control, and generation that a hybrid needs.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">The four advantages Roblox is betting on</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is one more advantage, and it is operational rather than technical. Even once the model runs in real time, Roblox will have to serve it to millions of players at once, and few companies have more practice keeping a system alive at that scale. Capacity is hard to predict when a game can jump from 3 million to 22 million players in a few weeks, so Roblox plans for sudden surges instead of assuming they will not come. Rather than throttling traffic when a system is under load, it runs a weekly exercise it calls Taco Tuesday, deliberately removing capacity from services in production to find the limits first. The test is automated, and any engineer can start one. Reliability is treated as everyone’s job, with executives on the same on-call rotation as engineers, holidays included.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What’s next</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An early version of Roblox Reality is expected later this year or early next, with cost and scaling still to solve before it can reach large numbers of players. The first quality target is 2K resolution at 60 frames per second, with 4K as the longer goal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The more important change is who gets to build photorealistic games. Because the heavy rendering happens on shared edge GPUs rather than on the creator’s machine or the player’s device, visual quality stops depending on the size of a team’s budget or the power of a player’s phone. A creator can get high-end results on an ordinary device. The goal Singh describes is for a two person studio to build something as rich as a large studio’s work, without having to trade complexity against visual quality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Singh expects the progress to arrive in large steps rather than small ones, and he expects world models to matter well beyond games. Roblox’s approach is worth watching because it does not wait for a video model to solve everything on its own. It gives the model the support it has always lacked: an engine that remembers the world, enforces its rules, and keeps it true for everyone playing.</span></p></div></div><div
