Either way it lands as a PR ready for review by morning.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>More complex development work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Build new telemetry integrations and verify they work</span></strong><span>. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ee1b5dc-d090-4931-b702-9d6b35f75331?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Lawrence Jones</span></a><span>, software engineer at Incident.io:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A lot of the AI runbook that we use to build new telemetry integrations uses loops such as executing the query, verifying that it executed correctly and iterating on the query plan/output format/whatever until it is happy with the outcome.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Do a long-running migration, mostly autonomously</span></strong><span>. Startup founder </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fea339ac-7a47-439f-86ab-f80bc8e52038?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Rafel Mendiola</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Recently, I converted my startup’s codebase from a regular React app to a React Native app using Expo.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two ways I could have done it:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the traditional software engineering style, I could have created a large epic with 50-100 different tickets. I started building myself the infrastructure for that, it felt like it was way too much work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What I did instead was create a skill that would let an agent figure out a small to medium-sized piece of work or piece of code to convert, given certain detection mechanisms and guidelines, and then do that conversion and keep track of the migration progress. Then I put that skill on a cron job. This was a lot easier to handle cognitively than managing a large migration plan. It also ran every 30 minutes, not nightly or weekly.”</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Productivity-related workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Daily tasks executed. </span></strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3143e70d-19e1-4cf6-9096-da54daa58717?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Aaron Stannard</span></a><span>, creator of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/613435ab-28eb-4a86-b9bc-50265dcfd437?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Akka.NET</span></a><span>:</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I use a reminder with my Netclaw instance to run both engineering and non-engineering things in a loop:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>1. Daily CRM triage </span><br><span>2. Support ticket SLA monitoring </span><br><span>3. Disk space management on my dev box </span><br><span>4. Triaging dependent PRs”</span></span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Daily and weekly automations. href="https://substack.com/redirect/adfedb71-efc2-49a0-b430-17bab1e3f2aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Matt Teixeria</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I have 4 main loops:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Daily: a feature, it looks at analytics, feedback, bugs etc</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Weekly: Product Market Fit Checker → goes over last week’s PMF survey and synthesizes actions to take “</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Disappointment and “tokenmaxxing”</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Plenty of devs shared that they tried loops but that it didn’t help them. Some common observations:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Human in the loop” works a lot better than letting the agent run by itself.</span></strong><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c9b1185-df4b-4426-9b7e-f94b3efdb024?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Kyle Straits</span></a><span>, founder at Stratis Data Labs:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I avoid loops. I had okay results with Ralph loops but nothing beats some well-defined skills, human in the loop (HITL), and an appropriate number of tools”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Lack of trust in the agent.</span></strong><span> Lead software engineer </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5c253f88-c90f-4d98-b080-515822aa476d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Anitha Mittapalli</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I find AI drifting or going off course several times and can’t trust it 100%. I use it every day, but still remain as an orchestrator.  It all depends on the type of tasks or problems you are solving. Thing is, work that is visual, subjective, architectural, or requires a lot of real-time design pivots, doesn’t always work well with autonomous agents or looping.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d9238f67-012c-42c9-96e3-090df974160d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jose Salvatierra</span></a><span>, founding engineer at Paper Run says the same:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Loops are handy for simple/low context tasks but it seems to break down as soon as things get complex and you need to guide the agent.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s hard to have a clear success criteria for complex work. </span></strong><span>Fractional CTO, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/24a29ac7-0ea9-4caa-bee5-4526e370281a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Carly Rector</span></a><span>, explains:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Complicated tasks rarely have clear success criteria you can fully define upfront... The examples of coding agents going away for weeks to build an [X] tend not to mention the time it takes to build the spec you give it... the job of specifying what you want to build is definitionally your job.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Why ‘loop engineer’ when tokens cost money?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A point of view exists that “loop engineering” is about incentivizing </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1402f920-39e7-4643-b083-6693a974c2c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>tokenmaxxing</span></a><span>. Plenty of devs spoke of their suspicion that AI labs are driven to incentivize more token usage, while loop engineering requires spending a lot of tokens. Plus, this new way of working is promoted from inside of OpenAI and Anthropic. Hence, there’s this suspicion that loop engineering is a plot to enrich AI labs by driving token usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true the incentives align, but I wonder if it’s something else:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Could it be that “designing loops” is more popular within AI labs because token budgets are absent there? </span></strong><span>Inside these places, devs are incentivized to experiment however they want.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, token costs are a concern elsewhere, and more places are</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c7f2871-2261-41cf-bfce-b184efcaa9bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> cutting back on token spend.</span></a><span> Devs on subsidized Claude Code and Codex plans will use primitives like /goal to start longer-running tasks, while those on a budget will consider the cost of the loop more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also where the idea of running open models on your own infra becomes more interesting because in this setting, the model is effectively “free” beyond the fixed setup fee, and suddenly tokenmaxxing (using GPUs at full capacity) is no longer economically silly!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Was looping a hack while tooling caught up?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Talking with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf842d32-1633-4712-bd38-c9f5a85addff?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Max Kanat-Alexander</span></a><span> – an executive distinguished engineer at Capital One, and formerly of LinkedIn – he made an interesting observation about how model shops keep improving their tooling:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think about the incentives that the model shops have in the long run. Those incentives always seem to be squarely aligned with “support people writing a single vague prompt and giving them what they want, without them having to do anything special or understand anything about the tool.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to me that anything you have to know about the tool would eventually become baked into its default workflow (or model capability would overtake it) if it really does get genuinely validated.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I agree with Max, OpenAI and Anthropic seem very good at launching DIY tools that take off because something is missing in Codex or Claude Code that needs a workaround. They simply build a version of the workaround into their products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps this points to why the loop engineering trend looks like being short-lived: if you have an ambitious project with a measurable goal, you can now one-shot it in a harness, and have long-running agents swarm and attempt to build it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Max had another sage point about why trends like “Ralph loops” and “loop engineering” might not last long:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s a theme of the last few years: there’s a trend that people get excited about which is then obviated because if it’s completely right, the model shops will inherently integrate it.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Does “context engineering” matter more for devs?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the time of publication, “loop engineering” seems as good as obsolete for most of us software engineers who build “regular” software. The tools have caught up and we can use the /goal or /loop prompts to do more ambitious, verifiable, tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But I reckon that designing loops will remain an important task at the AI infra level – and is probably why engineers at AI labs talk about it so much. </span></strong><span>It would be quite a lot of work to build a Ralph loop from scratch that you can ship in an AI harness like Codex, or a solution that’s resilient to a node running a crashing agent, is secure enough, auditable, etc. But if you do build this, you’ll learn plenty:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to decide when to start subagents, and how many of them to kick off</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to store the “global state” of the run: in files, memory, or in some other storage?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to avoid agents stepping on each other when working; for example, by using worktrees, working in the same filesystem but on different files, or something else?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How much of the context window to use, when to do </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d81f086-3f9d-4d48-b394-576a8481a375?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>context compaction/compression</span></a><span>, and other related stuff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and you’d solve many interesting problems!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Understanding “context engineering” can be useful when working with LLMs. </span></strong><span>Interest in Ralph loops started because the context window of LLMs is too small to hold large codebases, and with long-running, complex work the context window fills up. Also, the more you fill the context window, the less useful the LLM becomes because more errors compound and the agent “drifts.” Here’s my attempt at visualizing this:</span></p><div 16px;"><span>I hope it has been useful to look under the hood of “loop engineering.” If I wanted to be a bit cheeky in summary, this meme might sum up part of my view:</span></p><div used for decades?</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that would be a little unfair.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The reason “loop engineering” no longer matters for most devs is because AI harnesses are very quick in “one-shotting” more complex workflows. </span></strong><span>A year ago, it took a 30-minute read from Geoffrey Huntley to understand the theory of Ralph loops, and devs spent hours putting together their own looping environments. Then, Codex, Claude Code, and other AI harnesses built this functionality and abstracted it behind a simple command.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>So now, all complexity has been removed, and most devs no longer need to know much about looping or playing with context windows, unless building a harness, or needing to build a similar infra piece from scratch.</span><br><br></span><strong><span>A note of caution: there is a large amount of misleading AI slop on social media about loop engineering, so it helps to be able to spot the nonsense. </span></strong><span>Indeed, working on this article was the first time I have nearly fallen for AI replies to a mini-survey I ran on social media. I got lots of replies hyping up loop engineering, but offering no specifics. Sure enough, when I looked closer at the accounts posting these replies, they looked like they’re run by an AI bot. Here’s a couple such replies about loop engineering:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The loop is what runs when you’re not typing. it’s the agent deciding what to try next, running it, reading the result, deciding again. you’re not writing the steps anymore, you’re writing the objective and the constraints. that’s the paradigm shift” – AI-nonsense reply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/23052c49-514d-463e-a86f-225529395ba8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>from a founder</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Workflows have existed for years. What’s new is who owns the next step. In a traditional workflow, every stage waits for a person to decide what happens next. In a loop, the agent keeps planning, verifying, and correcting itself until it hits a stopping condition or asks for human judgment.” – another founder </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7168b3d-c462-419b-9dc6-311041c4b258?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>posting AI nonsense</span></a><span>.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s not just AI nonsense, but those posting about “loop engineering” are hard to relate as a “normal” software engineer. Here’s an “everyday” software engineer who experiments with AI, a lot, telling me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I feel a strange disconnect with the folks running loops. I usually cannot get my LLM to write even 200 - 500 lines without doing some major idiocy like returning a “fallback value” instead of an error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But on Twitter/X it’s a parallel reality where nobody writes or reads any code and runs 100 loops. I keep asking myself: am I doing it wrong?”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To this engineer: you’re probably not doing it wrong, but loops are not “magic” for most of us. </span><em><span>If you’re working building AI infra-like projects where you’re creating new, loop-like building blocks with agents doing clever stuff that was not possible before, this probably doesn’t apply to you.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope this walkthrough of loop engineering and its demise at the hands of progress – and the fact it appears to be disappearing as fast as it appeared – was useful. Do leave a comment on how you use “loops” and any use cases I missed.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwNzA0Mzc3NiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODQwNDkwNzEsImV4cCI6MjA5OTYyNTA3MSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.CP64l6k9PqatWnaAMblFmK_m_9-kjeJ7YeOtTlilINg?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. Each case requires a different direction with underlying trade-offs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The model learned to handle those trade-offs from people comparing answers thousands of times over. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let’s look at each stage in a bit more detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first stage is pretraining. The model reads an enormous amount of text and learns to predict the next word. In other words, it builds a broad sense of how language works and soaks up world knowledge along the way. What it gains is raw capability. What it still lacks is direction, because predicting the next word and answering your question are two different goals.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second stage is supervised fine-tuning, or SFT. We show the model thousands of example pairs, each an instruction together with a good response, and train it to imitate them. After this stage, the model follows instructions instead of continuing text. For example, if we ask a model to summarize a paragraph, it writes a proper summary. A raw model without SFT would have rambled on.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third stage teaches preferences, which will be the focus of the rest of this article.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Why does a model that already follows instructions need a third stage at all?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is because SFT works through imitation. The model sees a correct answer and learns to copy its shape, which holds up well when a question has one good answer, but runs into problems when a question has many possible answers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Consider a request like “explain how a hash map works”. A short answer and a long answer can both be excellent, and which one helps depends on who is asking. An example dataset can show one of those answers, while the trade-off between them stays invisible. Imitation teaches the model what a good answer looks like, but struggles to teach it how to weigh two good answers against each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The payoff is larger than it might appear at first. For example, when OpenAI built InstructGPT in 2022, human raters preferred answers from a 1.3 billion parameter aligned model over answers from the 175 billion parameter GPT-3, a model roughly a hundred times larger. The alignment stage mattered more than a hundredfold jump in size.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Nevertheless, the line between pretraining and SFT is cleaner in the example than in practice.  Some recipes blend the two, but the three-stage view is the right place to start.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Next up, we need a signal that captures the trade-off directly. That signal is comparison.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0fd3b3d6-fce9-471a-915d-fe0f15b0dcec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Introducing Attio: the agentic CRM. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Preferences</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Comparison turns a judgment call into something a model can learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A preference example is simple. We take one prompt, generate two responses, and ask a person which is better. The result is a small piece of data, a prompt with a winner and a loser. If we collect enough of these, a pattern emerges that captures the trade-offs accurately.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>The reason this works comes down to what people are good at. Writing the single ideal response to a tricky prompt is hard, and two skilled people would produce different versions. Judging which of two responses is better is far easier, and people agree with each other more often when they compare than when they create. This is why labeling teams compare outputs instead of writing perfect ones from scratch, which makes the data trustworthy enough to train on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the same comparison data InstructGPT collected, and the starting point for both methods we are about to compare. They differ in what they do with it, while the comparisons stay the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To clarify, the comparisons can come from another AI model in place of a person, an approach used in RLAIF and Constitutional AI. The overall mechanics stay the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us now look at the two different methods.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>RLHF</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>RLHF, short for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, learns from comparisons by training a separate scorer and then coaching the model to score well against it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the below diagram that shows the basic RLHF flow:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/47d74cf8-aa89-47d0-b430-3f9ffeb5f85c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It works in two moves once the comparisons are collected.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>First, we train a reward model. We take those prompt-with-a-winner examples and train a separate model to score any response, high for the kind people preferred and lower for the kind they passed over. The reward model turns scattered human judgments into a single function that grades fresh responses on its own.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Second, we use that scorer to improve the main model, which here we call the policy. The policy writes a response, the reward model scores it, and a reinforcement learning algorithm called PPO nudges the policy toward higher-scoring responses.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Reinforcement learning, in plain terms, means learning from a reward signal through trial and error in place of labeled examples. Run the loop many times, and the policy drifts toward the answers people prefer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Left to chase a score freely, a model will discover strange, degenerate text that games the scorer while reading badly. To guard against that, we keep a frozen copy of the starting model, the reference, and penalize the policy whenever it strays too far from it. This penalty, the KL term, lets the policy improve while staying close enough to fluent language to stay useful.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reward model, the policy, the frozen reference, and a value model that PPO uses internally add up to four models in play during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That is the source of RLHF’s reputation for being expensive, fiddly, and slow to get right. However, this is also the pipeline behind the first version of ChatGPT, and it produced the first generation of genuinely helpful assistants at considerable cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Running a separate reward model and a full RL loop is a lot of moving parts. In 2023, a study from Stanford showed that much of it can collapse into a single step.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>DPO</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO reaches the same goal with the same data, replacing the reward model and the RL loop with one training step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO stands for Direct Preference Optimization, and the name fits. Rather than train a scorer and then optimize against it, the method tunes the model directly on the comparison pairs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The mechanics sit close to ordinary supervised learning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For each comparison, DPO adjusts the model to raise the probability of the preferred response and lower the probability of the rejected one, measured against that same frozen reference from before. The whole thing becomes a single loss that would train the way you would train a classifier. This is far simpler and steadier than an RL loop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A common idea is that DPO removes the reward model, but what actually happens is subtler. The Stanford paper that introduced DPO carries the idea in its title that a language model is secretly a reward model. The reward signal is still present, but it now lives inside the policy itself rather than in a separate network.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/adcd9c85-55cb-45e7-a593-cd0c59336165?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" justify"><span>The approach proved itself quickly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Zephyr, a 7 billion parameter model trained with DPO on machine-generated comparisons, beat Llama 2 Chat 70B, the strongest open RLHF model at the time, on a standard chat benchmark. Since then, DPO has become a staple in the industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>By folding the reward into a single training step, DPO put alignment within reach of a small team on a modest budget, far from any large research cluster. A family of variants, such as SimPO, KTO, and ORPO, adjusts the objective in different ways. They share DPO’s core approach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>On cost and simplicity, DPO looks like a clear win. The catch is one it shares with RLHF, and it sits in the signal both methods trust.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Reward Hacking</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both methods rely on a signal that only approximates human judgment, and leaning too hard on it can also backfire at times.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reward model, whether trained explicitly in RLHF or folded into the policy in DPO, is a proxy. It approximates what people prefer. Like any approximation, it also has gaps. Optimize the model hard against that proxy, and it can start to exploit those gaps. In other words, the score climbs while the answers get worse.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Researchers at OpenAI measured this directly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>As the model optimizes against the proxy, true quality rises for a while, then peaks and slides backward even as the proxy score keeps climbing. They tied it to Goodhart’s law, the old observation that a measure stops being a good measure once it becomes the target.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>The everyday symptoms of this are familiar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Models pad answers with length because longer responses tend to score well, and they learn to agree with whatever view you express. This behavior is called sycophancy. Anthropic found that most of the time, both human raters and reward models prefer a confident, agreeable answer over a correct one, which sometimes means flattery in place of truth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The important part is that this trouble follows the data rather than the algorithm.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO inherits it just as RLHF does, because both learn from the same imperfect human judgments. Simpler training buys you a great deal, and this particular problem comes along for the ride. This is why your model sometimes agrees with you when you are clearly wrong. It learned that agreement tends to score well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The KL penalty we discussed earlier softens this by holding the model near its starting point, though it shrinks the problem rather than completely erasing it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the root trouble is an imperfect human signal, a natural question follows. Could we replace it with a signal that is exact? For a certain class of tasks, we can.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Verifiable Rewards</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When a program can check the answer, the human reward becomes optional, and that single fact reshaped the final training stages across 2025 and 2026.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some tasks have a checkable answer:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A math problem is right or wrong.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A piece of code passes its tests or fails them.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For these, we can replace the human-derived reward model with a verifier, a program that grades the result directly. The signal becomes exact and effectively free, clearing the proxy problem at its root for that work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DeepSeek pushed this idea furthest.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>They introduced an RL method called GRPO that drops one of the extra models PPO needs, and they trained their R1 reasoning model largely by rewarding correct final answers on math and code. The results matched the strongest closed reasoning models of the time. The model learned to reason by checking its own work, guided by a reward a calculator could supply.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The limit is that a verifier can grade a math proof. However, it stays silent on whether an answer is honest, kind, or appropriately cautious. Those qualities take many acceptable forms and resist any automatic test, the territory preference learning was built for. DeepSeek themselves kept reward models for the helpfulness and safety parts of R1, while verifiable rewards drove the reasoning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This gives us the rule for the whole landscape.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When a machine can check the answer, reach for verifiable rewards. When the answer is a matter of judgment, reach for preference learning, whether RLHF or DPO. The method follows the signal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We can retrace the path in a sentence each:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A raw model learns language and knowledge from pretraining.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Supervised fine-tuning teaches it to follow instructions by imitation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A third stage teaches preferences, because the questions that matter most often have several good answers and a real trade-off between them.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Comparison is the signal that captures that trade-off, and the two main methods both run on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>RLHF trains a separate reward model and optimizes against it with reinforcement learning, which is powerful and costly. On the other hand, DPO folds the same signal into a single training step, which is simpler and steadier while keeping the reward implicit rather than absent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both inherit the same catch, that a human signal is a proxy, and pushing on it too hard breeds sycophancy and quiet failures. And when a task has a checkable answer, verifiable rewards now sidestep the proxy entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: item.title: Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams

Will Larson

“When you talk about growing an organization, the conversation usually leads to hiring. While I believe hiring is a very important approach to growing organizations, I believe we reach for it too often. In order to prioritize hiring for scenarios where it’ll do the most good, over the past year I’ve developed a loose framework for reasoning about what a given team needs to increase performance.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams

item.title: Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering

Brian Houck

“Each paper tackles a different question. Some measure the productivity impact of AI coding assistants. Others examine how those gains propagate through the software delivery process, explore what developers actually want from future AI systems, or reconsider the kinds of debt we should be paying attention to in an AI-assisted world. Despite coming from different research groups and using very different methodologies, they all seem to be converging on the same underlying story.”

#Management AI
item.description: Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering

item.title: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

Steve Huynh

“After participating in many such conversations, both through my podcast and during my time at Amazon, I have recognized a handful of patterns that have held over the decades and across different companies. What follows is my running list of those patterns, the ones that keep surfacing whenever I sit down with someone elite. There are five of them, and I explain the gap between what they do and where most other people stop.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

item.title: Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t

“In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned.”

#IndustryTrends AI
item.description: Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t

item.title: When AI Costs More Than The Engineer
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
When AI Costs More Than The Engineer

Tomasz Tunguz

“Anthropic spends 2.3x its payroll on compute — $515k per engineer per year at today's $224k fully-loaded salary. The top 1% of software companies spend $89k, the median $137. Three 2029 scenarios bracket how that gap closes.”

#Management
item.description: When AI Costs More Than The Engineer

item.title: On Data Quality
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
On Data Quality

Abraham Thomas

“Data quality. We love it, we want it, we praise it, we aspire to it. Even in these benighted and degenerate times, if there’s one belief that unites all sensible individuals, it is the belief that data quality is a Good Thing. It’s a pity, then, that nobody seems to know what data quality is.”

#DataEngineering Architecture
item.description: On Data Quality

item.title: A Software Architecture Reading List
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Software Architecture Reading List

Dr Andrew Leigh

“Dr Andrew Leigh reflects on 25 years of professional experience as a software architect and offers his insights and a reading list of recommendations.”

#Books Architecture
item.description: A Software Architecture Reading List

In 2026, we are seeing a huge increase in the number of our customers that are using voice as a front-end, so we’re also leaving the chatbot era of AI.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The old shape was a chatbot. The user types, the agent types back, and it can only answer questions. The new shape is an agent that does meaningful work on the user’s behalf. It books the meeting, runs the analysis, sends the email, files the ticket. The user might not type at all because the front end can be voice. For example, Foundry’s Voice Live lets a team turn an existing text agent into a voice agent without rebuilding it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Production is where the cracks open. Real users ask things you didn’t anticipate. Documents the agent depends on go stale. New edge cases emerge that never appeared in your eval dataset. A model update changes the agent’s behavior subtly, and nobody notices until a customer complains. Without identity controls, the agent runs as a shared system principal and there’s no audit trail when something goes wrong. Without guardrails, it confidently says something it shouldn’t. Without observability, you can’t tell whether quality is improving or degrading. None of these problems showed up in the prototype. All of them show up in production.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 Agent Runtime</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Above the model is the agent runtime, which is what turns a model into an agent. The runtime handles the orchestration loop, the tool calls, the conversation state, and the protocol the rest of the harness speaks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not every step in that loop should run through the model. A well-built agent sends only the parts that need reasoning to the LLM and leaves the rest to ordinary code, since a database lookup or a purpose-built extraction model is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than asking a model to do the same work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The number of agent frameworks keeps growing, from open-source options like LangChain, LangGraph, and CrewAI to vendor-built runtimes. The principle that matters is framework neutrality. An agent built on one framework should be portable to another without rewriting the surrounding harness. Foundry, for example, lets agents run on any framework interchangeably.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Identity Layer</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once agents start taking real actions inside an organization, they need their own identities. They need their own role assignments and their own audit trails, because a misbehaving agent has to be bounded by the same access controls that bound a misbehaving employee. The industry is still converging on how to do this well, and the answer most platforms are landing on is to extend an existing enterprise identity system to treat agents as a new class of principal rather than inventing a parallel system. For example, Foundry extends Entra, Microsoft’s enterprise identity platform, to treat agents this way. This is the access-control primitive; later in the article, the section on giving agents a place to act shows what an agent does once it has one of these identities.</span></p><div That’s the job of the context layer. While every other layer in the harness exists to let the agent run, context is what lets it run correctly. An agent without good context might hallucinate. It will give an answer, but the answer will be wrong in ways that are hard to detect because the agent itself doesn’t know what it doesn’t know. Marco was explicit that giving agents the context they need to actually work is one of the hardest problems his team is solving, and the one Microsoft is reasonably passionate about getting right.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The standard answer of the last two years, classic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), was never designed to. Classic RAG is a one-shot pattern. You take the user’s question, embed it, search a single index, return the top-k results, and pass them to the model. It works for simple questions against a small, clean corpus. It breaks the moment the question is ambiguous, the corpus is heterogeneous, the right answer requires combining sources, or the first retrieval comes back empty. The agent has no way to recover from a bad retrieval, and as Marco put it, when RAG isn’t working well, the whole agent isn’t working well. One-shot is the wrong shape for the problem.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each IQ is a headless service that agents call through MCP. Two engineering ideas run through them. The first, retrieval-as-a-subagent, is the pattern behind all four. The second, giving an agent an identity and a place to act, is specifically what Work IQ adds on top of retrieval so that an agent can do work, not just find information.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Retrieval-as-a-Subagent</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The technical idea behind a production context layer is to wrap retrieval in an agentic loop. Instead of a single function call that runs one query against one index and returns the top-k, retrieval becomes a small agent of its own. It plans which sources to query, executes the queries, evaluates the results against the original question, and decides whether to return them, refine the query, or try a different source. Retrieval stops being a lookup and becomes an iterative process that can recover from a bad first pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Foundry IQ is the cleanest example of this in production today. The figure below shows the workflow when an agent calls it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The last step is the one most worth paying attention to. When iteration runs out, Foundry IQ returns a structured “I don’t know” instead of forcing an answer. Classic RAG has no fallback and the model hallucinates something plausible. Foundry IQ gives the calling agent a clear signal that retrieval failed, which it can act on, rather than a confident wrong answer that’s hard to detect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So far this is all about data. The same loop applies to tools. An agent with a few tools can list them all in its prompt. One with dozens can’t. Listing them all burns context on every call and slows the model down as it scans the list. The fix is similar to agentic retrieval. Instead of exposing every tool, the agent searches for the right one, gets it back, and calls it. Foundry exposes this as tool search, and it’s the pattern OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s agents have converged on too. So the same retrieval loop that pulls in knowledge also pulls in capability. The agent looks up what it needs at the moment it needs it instead of carrying everything up front.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other IQs rely on the same pattern too. Fabric IQ runs agentic retrieval over structured data, with the loop planning queries against OneLake tables and the Fabric data agent rather than against text indexes. Web IQ runs the same loop over the open web at sub-second latency. The retrieval-as-subagent idea is the architectural commonality across all of them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>An Identity and a Place to Act</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retrieval gets the agent the right information. But information alone doesn’t finish a task. An agent that knows the customer is unhappy still has to write the apology email and refund the order. To do that responsibly, the agent needs two things. An identity the organization can see, and a surface where it can take action.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The identity is the access-control primitive from the identity layer earlier. Without it, every action is anonymous or on behalf of a user who lent the agent their identity. Logs show that “the AI did it” and the audit trail collapses, which is unworkable for any regulated enterprise. The fix is to treat agents as their own class of principal, sitting in the same directory as employees, with their own role assignments and their own audit trails. A misbehaving agent gets bounded by the same access controls that bound a misbehaving employee.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The action surface is what makes the identity meaningful. An agent that exists in the directory but has no way to send an email or update a document isn’t doing work. The surface has to expose the same actions a person already takes inside the organization, so that an agent operating on top of it can read inboxes, send messages, schedule meetings, and edit shared documents. In Microsoft’s case, identity is handled through Entra and the action surface is Work IQ. An agent can now have a named directory entry, report to a manager in the org chart, and own its mailbox.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">An agent with its own identity and an action surface</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Identity bounds what an agent is allowed to reach. Guardrails bound what flows through it once it acts. A chatbot only had to screen the user’s prompt and the model’s reply. An agent has more surface to defend, because it also reads tool outputs and retrieved documents, and any of those can carry an instruction the user never typed. That is how indirect prompt injection works. A line like “ignore your previous instructions” sits hidden inside a document the agent ingests, and the agent treats it as a command. The fix is to move guardrails to the tool boundary, screening tool inputs and tool outputs rather than just the model’s input and output. In Microsoft’s case, Foundry runs its own classifiers at the tool-call and tool-response level, on top of whatever safety the model already has. Since these controls live on a shared tool layer rather than inside each agent, a team configures them once and every agent that uses those tools inherits them, instead of re-implementing the same guardrails, credentials, and policies agent by agent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway for any team building this is that retrieval, action, and the guardrails around both need to be designed as first-class layers. Retrieval should be a loop that recovers from bad lookups, action should run under an identity the organization recognizes with an audit trail to match, and guardrails should sit at the tool boundary rather than only at the model’s edges.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Evaluate Production Agents</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Context is half of what determines whether an agent survives production. Evaluation is the other half. An agent with the right context can still drift, regress, or fail in new ways as traffic patterns change. Evaluation is what closes the loop. It’s the system that tells you when something has changed, and the system that tells you whether the agent is doing what it’s supposed to do.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Continuous Evaluation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most teams treat evaluation as a pre-ship checkbox. They run a test suite once, see green, and ship. That works for traditional software because traditional software is deterministic. An agent is not. The same prompt against the same model can produce different responses, the model itself changes when the provider releases an update, and the data the agent retrieves from changes daily. A pre-ship test suite catches a snapshot of behavior, not a guarantee of it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Continuous evaluation closes that gap by running against live traffic, sampling real user interactions, scoring them on whatever criteria the team has defined, and surfacing results into the same observability pipeline that already handles infrastructure incidents. In Foundry, this is built in. When quality regresses, the team finds out from the same alerting system that pages them when a service goes down. The same evaluations can also run earlier, as a gate in the deployment pipeline, catching a regression before it ships.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Rubric-Based Evaluation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Continuous evaluation tells you when something has changed. The harder problem is knowing whether what the agent is doing is right in the first place. Most evaluation systems today rely on generic metrics like groundedness, coherence, and task completion. The metrics are useful but they have a ceiling. As Marco put it, generic metrics tell you whether the agent works. They don’t tell you whether the agent works right.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider an agent that helps users book restaurant reservations. It is the kind of wrong-action failure from the opening, seen up close. A generic metric can tell you that the agent called the booking tool successfully and returned a reservation. But it can’t tell you whether the agent did the right things along the way. Did it ask the user what time they wanted when the user only said “a table for two tomorrow”? Did it check the booking system to confirm the table was actually available before claiming a 6pm slot? A reservation that gets created without those checks is technically a success against generic metrics and a failure in the user’s eyes.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The way to close that gap is to evaluate the agent against the specific behaviors it should be showing, not just generic metrics. The common approach is rubric-based evaluation. A rubric is a specific, use-case-tied check that asks a yes-or-no question about something the agent should be doing. For the restaurant agent, the rubrics might look like:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When the user gives a partial request, does the agent ask for the missing information?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Before claiming a reservation is available, does the agent verify availability against the booking system?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>After making a booking, does the agent confirm the details back to the user?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In practice, the eval system runs the agent against a set of test interactions, scores each rubric per interaction, and rolls the results up. The team sees not just whether the agent works but which specific behaviors it’s getting right and which it isn’t. Rubrics work better than generic metrics because the team that owns the agent writes them, so they reflect what the agent is actually supposed to do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Writing them by hand isn’t the only path. Foundry can draft a rubric by reading the agent’s configuration and its production traces, proposing the dimensions worth scoring from how the agent actually behaves. The team still owns and edits the result, but it starts from real traffic instead of a blank page.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: steps</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft has built rubric-based evaluation into its Agent Optimizer suite. The Optimizer handles the rubric side of the loop and also makes the rubrics actionable by automatically improving the agent itself when a rubric fails. It can rewrite the system prompt to make the missing behavior more explicit, adjust how the agent uses its tools, or change which sources the agent prioritizes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What it tunes goes beyond the prompt. It can also swap the underlying model and tune the agent’s skills. Rather than testing one fix at a time, it produces several candidates in parallel, scores each against the rubrics, and promotes the best one as a new agent version. The same loop that measures the agent now improves it. It becomes a self-improving loop.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0
