0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For any team running agents in production, evaluation isn’t a phase that ends. It’s a layer that runs alongside the agent, with rubrics that evolve as the agent’s job evolves and an optimizer that turns regressions into actionable changes instead of manual fixes. The team’s job stops being to write the perfect agent on day one and starts being to keep the agent honest as the world around it changes. That’s what production AI actually looks like, and it’s the second half of the harness Foundry is built around.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Key Lesson for Other Teams</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The harness mattering as much as the model is the thread that ran through the whole conversation. The reason context is hard, the reason evaluation is hard, the reason a working prototype doesn’t survive production, is that the work most teams treat as “around the model” is actually what determines whether the agent works. Treating the harness as something you add later is the most common reason an enterprise agent never makes it to production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The practical version of that lesson for a team building its own context layer is to take the two architectural ideas from earlier in this article seriously, even if you don’t use Foundry. Retrieval should be agentic. Calls to your retrieval layer should hide a planner-driven, multi-source, retry-capable subagent that can recover from a bad lookup instead of breaking on one. And agents that take actions should have identities the organization recognizes, with audit trails that survive a compliance review. Both of these are buildable on top of any platform.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What’s Next</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Marco thinks about the future of AI by watching what’s about to become possible in the next year, not what’s ten years away. He tracks the moment a capability stops being a research demo or a developer tool and becomes something an ordinary person can use. The pattern he watches most closely is the one where capabilities that used to require a CLI coding agent become available to everyone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This pattern has been playing out for the last eight months. Capabilities that used to require a developer to wire up inside a coding agent, things like writing a document from natural language, managing a calendar, or running a custom workflow, are now showing up in tools. Skills, which started as a coding-agent concept, are now in Excel for tasks like financial analysis and private equity workflows. Marco’s expectation is that this pattern keeps accelerating, with more developer-only capabilities crossing into general use over the next year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>The bigger shift he sees coming is toward agents that improve themselves. The architectural pieces are global and local memory, plus skills, plus the kind of behaviors that let an agent retain what it learns about a user and apply it automatically. Copilot CLI’s new Chronicle feature is an early version. If Marco always commits his Git repos to GitHub immediately after creating them, Chronicle learns that and starts doing it for him without being asked. Marco’s bet is that this combination, applied to the kinds of agents enterprises are already deploying, is the story of the next year. Not science fiction. Just the next set of capabilities crossing into general use.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: item.title: Small programming tricks
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Small programming tricks

Will Keleher

4 minutes by Will Keleher Small tricks and shortcuts add up to meaningful gains in engineering productivity. Things like fuzzy shell history search, git pickaxe, or knowing a single command to spin up a local server can save real time without requiring deep background knowledge. The same applies inside companies, where knowing who to ask or where to find a doc can be just as valuable. Sharing one tip a day with your team is a simple way to spread this kind of knowledge.
item.description: Small programming tricks

item.title: When ‘if’ slows you down, avoid it
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
When ‘if’ slows you down, avoid it

Christof Kaser

4 minutes by Christof Kaser Branch mispredictions slow CPUs down because they force the processor to discard queued work and start over. Writing branchless code removes unpredictable jumps and lets the CPU run at full speed. A simple filter loop rewritten to use a conditional increment instead of an if statement ran nearly 10 times faster on an Apple M1. Compilers cannot make this change automatically because they cannot safely assume unconditional memory writes are always allowed.
item.description: When ‘if’ slows you down, avoid it

item.title: Running an obfuscated bash script from Uniqlo's tee
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Running an obfuscated bash script from Uniqlo's tee

Tristan Sherliker

6 minutes by Tristan Sherliker A Uniqlo t-shirt made in partnership with Akamai contains a real bash script printed on the back, encoded in base64. After carefully transcribing and decoding it, the script turns out to be a harmless Easter egg that displays a colorful animated "Peace for All" message in the terminal. Akamai designed the shirt as a nod to the early internet era, with the code serving as a reference to Linux.
item.description: Running an obfuscated bash script from Uniqlo's tee

item.title: Virtual memory from first principles
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Virtual memory from first principles

about 1 hour by Abhinav Upadhyay Abhinav provides a practical introduction to virtual memory, explaining its core mechanisms, including address translation, demand paging, copy-on-write, memory mapping, and page reclaim. He also explores their impact on system performance, memory management, and observability, equipping readers with a mental model for building and debugging data-intensive systems.
item.description: Virtual memory from first principles

4 minutes by Jim Grey Getting into the software industry matters more than getting the perfect role right away. Taking jobs in support, QA, or technical writing puts you close to real problems and real people. Relationships built through good work open doors that portfolios alone cannot. item.title: Memory discipline and GC awareness in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Memory discipline and GC awareness in .NET

Bipin Joshi

.NET apps rely on garbage collection, but frequent collection cycles cause latency spikes and wasted CPU time. Short-lived objects that survive a collection get promoted to more expensive memory tiers, quietly hurting performance under load. Tools like dotnet-trace and BenchmarkDotNet help find the real sources of memory pressure. Practical fixes include using structs, Span, ArrayPool, and ValueTask to cut unnecessary allocations and keep collections rare.
item.description: Memory discipline and GC awareness in .NET

item.title: Zero-code validations in your .NET API
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Zero-code validations in your .NET API

Pavel Kalandra

Pavel explains how strong types can replace repeated validation in .NET APIs. Instead of checking the same values in multiple layers, inputs are converted once into types that guarantee valid data. This reduces duplicate code, improves readability, strengthens type safety, and makes APIs easier to maintain. The approach also works with JSON, OpenAPI, Entity Framework Core, and testing with minimal setup.
item.description: Zero-code validations in your .NET API

item.title: Getting inherited controller routes to work in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Getting inherited controller routes to work in ASP.NET Core

Rick Strahl

Inheriting ASP.NET controllers with attribute routes can cause duplicate route errors. When a concrete base controller class is subclassed, ASP.NET registers routes from both the base and child classes, causing ambiguous route failures. Using an abstract base class prevents this, as ASP.NET skips abstract classes during route scanning. For concrete base classes, you can implement IActionDescriptorProvider to detect and remove the duplicate base class routes after ASP.NET completes its route discovery.
item.description: Getting inherited controller routes to work in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Improvements to reading process outputs
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Improvements to reading process outputs

Andrew Lock

.NET 11 adds new APIs that make reading output from child processes much safer and simpler. Earlier versions made it easy to accidentally cause deadlocks when reading stdout and stderr. New methods like ReadAllText, ReadAllLines, and RunAndCaptureText handle the complexity for you, covering both simple capture scenarios and cases where you need to react to output as it arrives.
item.description: Improvements to reading process outputs

item.title: The N+1 query problem in EF Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The N+1 query problem in EF Core

Chris Woodruff

Loading 200 database rows can silently trigger 201 queries when navigation properties are accessed in a loop. This is the N+1 problem, and it shows up in four forms: lazy loading loops, explicit query loops, serializer storms, and write-side save loops. The fix starts with counting queries using an interceptor, then setting a query budget in your tests. And the most popular article from the last issue was: * How to guide agents during production investigations with .NET
item.description: The N+1 query problem in EF Core

takes your command and sends it as an API call to the Docker daemon (dockerd) running on the host.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>dockerd checks whether the nginx image is already on disk. If it is not, it pulls it from a registry like Docker Hub or ECR. Then it prepares the container config.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>dockerd does not start the container directly. It passes the request to containerd, which manages the container lifecycle. containerd prepares the runtime files and assembles a bundle made of the OCI config and the root filesystem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>containerd then calls runc. runc reads the bundle, creates the Linux namespaces and mounts defined in the config, and starts the process inside them. Once the process is running, runc exits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The running container is a regular Linux process with its own PID, network, and mount namespaces. Its filesystem is a stack of read-only image layers with a writable layer on top, so changes inside the container do not modify the image.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Isolation comes from kernel features. Namespaces separate processes, cgroups limit CPU and memory, and network namespaces give the container its own interfaces. There is no guest OS and no hypervisor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over to you: where do most of your container issues show up, the image, networking, or resource limits?</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>git merge vs git rebase</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both commands get your changes into main. main approaches compare when the dataset is large.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most pagination implementations start with offset and page numbers. You ask for “?page=3&size=10” and the database skips 20 rows, then returns 10. Simple to build and easy to explain. The issue is that the database still reads every row it skips. Page 5 is fast. Page 5000 is slow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keyset pagination handles deep pages much better. Instead of counting rows, you tell the server to return items after ID 101. The query goes straight to that point using the index, so page 1 and page 10,000 take the same time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Continuation tokens are common in large APIs like S3 and YouTube. The server returns a token, you send it back on the next request, and it resumes from where the last response ended. It hides the cursor logic from the client. The token is tied to the filters and sort order from the original request, so the client must keep using the same parameters until the pagination ends.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Time-based pagination works well for feeds and logs. You ask for items before a timestamp and read backwards. Add a secondary field, like an ID, for rows that share the same timestamp. justify"><span>Here’s how it works:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Step 1: Understanding The Question and Making a Plan</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It all starts with the query, something like “Analyze the competitive landscape of AI agents in 2026. The system doesn’t just dive in blindly. First, it may ask clarifying questions to understand exactly what is needed. Then, it generates a plan and breaks the big question down into smaller and manageable tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Step 2: Sub-Agents Get to Work</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Each small task gets assigned to a sub-agent, which is basically a mini AI worker with a specific job. For example, one sub-agent might be tasked with finding the latest Nvidia earnings. It figures out which tools to use, such as searching the web, browsing a specific page, or even run code to analyze data. All of this happens through a secure layer of APIs and services that connect the AI to the outside world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Step 3: Putting it All Together</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once all the sub-agents finish their tasks, a Synthesizer Agent takes over. It aggregates everything, identifies key themes, plans an outline, and removes any redundant or duplicate information. At the same time, a Citation Agent makes sure every claim is linked back to its source and properly formatted. The end result is a polished, well-cited final output ready for use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;text-align: item.title: In Job Interviews, Keep Your Backstory Short
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
In Job Interviews, Keep Your Backstory Short

Wes Kao

“The problem is, when you spend too much time describing the situation (i.e. the context or background), you take time away from the other parts of STAR, all of which are more interesting and relevant. The situation should be a brief set up, so you can let the other parts of your STAR story really shine.”

#Communication CareerGrowth InterviewAdvice
item.description: In Job Interviews, Keep Your Backstory Short

item.title: Ownership
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Ownership

Thorsten Ball

“Just had a (great) conversation about ownership and engineering here and I realized that I often use the phrase “ownership” or allude to it, but haven’t explained what “ownership” means to me in a while.”

#Management Culture
item.description: Ownership

item.title: The Mario Meeting
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Mario Meeting

Michael Lopp

“Everyone cares about the compensation (base salary, bonus, and stock). That’s the data they care about, but where did this pile of compensation come from? Who decided how big it is? And how is it allocated? It is a long, complicated, and large process that began over a year ago. And as a Senior Leader, it’s your job to figure it out.”

#Leadership Management Compensation
item.description: The Mario Meeting

item.title: Software Engineering At The Tipping Point
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Software Engineering At The Tipping Point

Adam Bender

Adam explores software ecology as a framework for understanding sociotechnical systems. By examining the impact of emerging technologies and rapid growth on developer ecosystems, he investigates how culture and technical choices navigate the challenges of scaling environments.

#IndustryTrends Scale Architecture
item.description: Software Engineering At The Tipping Point

item.title: Software Design In The Agentic Age: Place Your Bets
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Software Design In The Agentic Age: Place Your Bets

Mathias Verraes

“This week, I participated in Thoughtworks’ Future of Software Engineering retreat in Engelberg, Switzerland. It was an invite-only event with about 60 industry leaders, hosted by Martin Fowler. The event used an open space format, where all sessions had the form of group debates, mostly focused on agentic development. Here are some of my observations on the changing role of software design.”

#IndustryTrends Architecture Agents
item.description: Software Design In The Agentic Age: Place Your Bets

item.title: How to Make Architecture Decisions: RFCs, ADRs, and Getting Everyone Aligned
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to Make Architecture Decisions: RFCs, ADRs, and Getting Everyone Aligned

Lukas Niessen

“The thing is, architecture decisions are different from regular code decisions. They’re harder to reverse, they affect more people, and they often involve trade-offs that aren’t purely technical. You need buy-in. You need the right people in the room. And you need a process that doesn’t turn into endless meetings or bikeshedding. Here’s the approach I’ve found works well, both in my consulting work and in teams I’ve led.”

#Leadership Architecture
item.description: How to Make Architecture Decisions: RFCs, ADRs, and Getting Everyone Aligned

item.title: Cost Attribution In Discord’s API
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Cost Attribution In Discord’s API

Jim Benton

“One observability gap that we wanted to improve last year was our understanding of how hosting costs were allocated across product features. For example, how much does it cost to operate the parts of API that are used to send and receive messages? Start a stream? Send a friend a Nitro gift?”

#DeepDive Metrics Infrastructure
item.description: Cost Attribution In Discord’s API

style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: resolution, a WebSocket client, Node.js implementations and many modules</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, Bun has 22 million monthly downloads, and software like Claude Code and OpenCode depend on it, while hosting providers like Vercel, Railway and DigitalOcean do first-party support for Bun.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Why a rewrite?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Zig is not a memory safe language, and memory-related bugs occurred continuously.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Jarrod </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4498dc0f-4233-452a-ba5f-58000f3e6530?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>lists</span></a><span> memory-related bugs in the latest version of Bun: memory leaks, crashes due to memory issues, heap-out-of-bounds writes, and so on. This was after the Bun team patched the Zig compiler to reduce memory-related issues, and put end-to-end memory leak tests in place. As Jarrod says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Our bugfix list felt bad and I was tired of going to sleep worrying about crashes in Bun. I don’t blame Zig for that - other users of Zig don’t have the bugs we had, and mixing GC with manually-managed memory is an uncommon enough thing for software to need that no language really designs for it. (...)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For Bun, correctly handling the lifetimes of garbage-collected values and manually-managed values has been a major source of stability issues - most often small memory leaks and occasionally crashes. Every memory allocation has to be meticulously reviewed. Where do these bytes get freed? How do we ensure it only gets freed once? Did we check for JavaScript exceptions properly? Is this garbage-collected pointer visible to the conservative stack scanner? Is this garbage collected memory or manually managed memory?”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Moving to a memory-safe, yet performant language could eliminate such errors, and Rust is one such language that fitted the bill. Jarrod:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A large percentage of bugs from that list are use-after-free, double-free, and “forgot to free” in an error path. In safe Rust, these are compiler errors and RAII-like automatic cleanup with Drop. Compiler errors are a better feedback loop than a style guide.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, doing a </span><em><span>full</span></em><span> rewrite on Rust has always been a terrible idea. Or at least, it used to be, because of how unberabaly long it would have taken:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>There are two problems with rewrites: they take too long, and they take waaaay too long. </span></strong><span>A dev who has done rewrites probably knows how things tend to go:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Make an educated guess about how long it will take; say, nine months.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Nine months later, there’s still another ~6 months to go because new functionality is added to the </span><em><span>original</span></em><span> codebase, and now that new functionality needs to be added in!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>By 15 months in, there’s still months left to go for the same reason!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the end, you manage to mandate a “feature freeze” for two months and finish the rewrite in ~18 months, if lucky. The original nine-month estimate can end up taking 2+ years.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarrod likened rewriting Bun in Zig to this:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Historically, rewrites are a terrible idea. Excluding comments, Bun is 535,496 lines of Zig.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A rewrite in another language would take a small team of engineers a full year.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A year of zero user-facing impact is not a realistic option we could consider. So, enforcement through code-style to fix stability issues was our best bet, and was our plan when we added Rust-inspired smart pointers to Bun’s codebase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But honestly, I didn’t want to do it. Homegrown smart pointers offer worse ergonomics than Rust, with none of the guarantees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What if, instead, I spend a week testing if Anthropic’s new model [Fable] can rewrite Bun in Rust?”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Rewriting Bun with Fable</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unsurprisingly, the rewrite was not as simple as typing a prompt like: “Claude, rewrite Bun in Rust. Make zero mistakes.” Instead, this is how Jarrod did it:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #1: Prep work.</span></strong><span> Three hours of intense prep work with Claude, explained</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Jarrod:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Before writing any code, I spent about 3 hours talking to Claude about how to map patterns from our Zig codebase closely to Rust. Claude serialized this discussion into a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2985c8a6-2c62-4c42-a15c-72841a6ecbc8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>PORTING.md</span></a><span> document, which ended up </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81d3531d-2233-431f-ae51-3b59369e0cfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on Hacker News</span></a><span> [as the Zig → Rust porting guide]”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This guide is a 600-line file with instructions like:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ground rules:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>No </span><strong><span>tokio</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>rayon</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>hyper</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>async-trait</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>futures</span></strong><span>. No std::fs, std::net, std::process. Bun owns its event loop and syscalls. (Rust core/std slice, iter, mem, fmt, and core::ffi are fine — only the I/O-touching modules are banned.)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>No </span><strong><span>async fn</span></strong><span>. Everything is callbacks + state machines, same as the Zig.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Borrow-checker reshaping is allowed.</span></strong><span> When matching Zig flow yields overlapping &mut, capture the needed scalar (.len(), index) into a local, drop the borrow, then re-borrow. Do NOT reach for raw pointers just to silence borrowck; leave // PORT NOTE: reshaped for borrowck so Phase B diff readers aren’t confused.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a series of instructions that makes sense to someone who’s expert in Rust.</span><em><span> If you want to learn more, we cover </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d64aaaeb-e264-4b2d-a36b-a586e73d99b7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Rust basics and why Rust is different, with Alice Ryhl.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #2: Trial run + adversarial review. </span></strong><span>Asking Claude to rewrite three files of 1,448 total number of files. After the rewrite, Jarrod ran two separate adversarial reviews with Claude to critique the result, in separate sessions than the one that Claude made the changes in.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #3: split up the work across 64 AI agents. </span></strong><span>Jarrod split up the job so that agents worked on files independent from one another, in parallel.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #4: iron out issues with the run (~1 day). </span></strong><span>When Jarrod attempted to run all this, agents kept getting in each other’s way:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I asked Claude to loop the workflow on all 1,448 .zig files, and about 2 minutes in, one Claude ran git stash before committing. Another ran git stash pop. And then git reset HEAD --hard. They were stepping on each other! And if I put each Claude into a separate worktree, I would run out of disk space because Bun’s git repository is too big and eventually the changes will need to be compiled and seen together.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, I asked Claude to edit the workflow to instruct Claude to never run git stash or git reset or any git command that doesn’t commit a specific file at once. No cargo either. No slow commands at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then, Claude resumed the workflows. And it was working! Too slowly, so I split it into just 4 workflow shards each with their own worktree (4 worktrees total), each running 16 Claudes committing and pushing files.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #5: have it run and wait ~2 days. </span></strong><span>The parallel agents went to work, and completed the rewrite of 535,496 lines of Zig code over the course of two days. Each commit was checked by two adversarial reviews, before being committed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #7: fix ~1,600 compiler errors (~12 hours).</span></strong><span> The rewrite was completed, but nothing compiled. Going crate-by-crate (‘crate’ is Rust’s concept of a top-level compilation unit), Jarrod had Claude fix compiler errors. </span><em><span>This alone would be a herculean task for an engineer, but not for Claude</span></em><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Fixing the cyclical dependencies revealed about 16,000 compiler errors. A massive number for 1 human, but not a crazy number for 64 Claude’s at once.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To maximize parallelism, the workflow looped over each crate.</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>For each crate, run cargo check, group the output by file and save the errors to a file</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fix all the compiler errors within that crate</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2 adversarial reviewers for the crate’s changes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1 fixer applies the fixes”</span></p></li></ul></blockquote><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px The next step was to get these tests to </span><em><span>run </span></em><span>without compilation errors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #9: get the test suite to pass CI (~3 days). </span></strong><span>Once the tests were running (and failing), the next step was to fix the code, so that the tests could pass. This took two days.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Step #10: Done in 11 days! </span></strong><span>After all the tests passed and Jarrod verified that everything worked as expected, he merged the changes. The whole process took 11 days, from planning to the finish.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How repeatable is this process?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The rewrite cost a whopping $165,000 with API pricing. </span></strong><span>With Fable’s API prices, the rewrite consumed 5.9 billion uncached input tokens, 690 million output tokens, and 72 billion cached input token reads. Anthropic sells API tokens at a margin as its business, so the cost of the rewrite for it was lower. It’s a large amount: the equivalent of the annual base salary for a software engineer at a mid-tier company in the US!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then again, could have an engineer done </span><em><span>all this work </span></em><span>in a year? Probably not, and Mitchell Hashimoto </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d5bd5431-0105-448f-bbd1-5875bef8b561?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>says the same</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“On the cost, I think $165,000 at API pricing for Fable (didn’t verify) is an incredible deal. There’s absolutely no way an engineer with that salary would’ve been able to achieve the milestones Claude did in 11 days. No way. (Even if you break it down to N engineers paid $165K total in 11 days it doesn’t math out)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This does, however, also reconfirm my own biases which is that Fable in particular is most excellent at hard, focused tasks with clear reward functions. I’ve been tweeting about this recently.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>What if AI enables rewrites and migrations that wouldn’t have been considered before? </span></strong><span>The idea of rewriting Bun in Rust without AI was impractical, admits Jarrod:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“By hand, I think this would’ve taken three engineers with full context on the codebase about a year, during which time we wouldn’t be able to improve Node.js compatibility, fix bugs, fix security issues or implement new features. We never would’ve done that. The realistic alternative was to do nothing and keep fixing the bugs at the top of this post forever.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A rewrite or migration taking months or years is why so many of these projects never happen. Let’s take aside the cost for a minute and consider this question: if AI can shorten a one-year rewrite to a week: would you do it?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the answer is “hell, yes:” a blueprint now exists in the form of the Bun migration on how to do it. There are some caveats not detailed in the post, though:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>You need an engineer who is </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> motivated and knows the codebase very well</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>You need an </span><em><span>extremely</span></em><span> robust test suite, so when the test suite passes, you know it works</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>You need to be willing to invest a lot in tokens, not knowing how well it all will work</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fairness, #3 is the weakest point because we know LLMs are pretty good at “mundane” work like code migrations. With a good test suite (#2) and a motivated engineer to iron out things (#1), you’ll more likely than not succeed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The remaining question is how much can be spent. It will likely not be $165K: and costs can be reduced with a simpler project, or by being thoughtful about model usage. For example, do high-level planning with the most expensive model, and cheaper ones for coding and review tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Migrations with AI are surely speeding up, but only when projects are well-engineered like Bun’s has been.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Anthropic’s Fable, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, Cursor’s Grok 4.5, Meta’s Muse</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s been a flurry of model news the past week:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Fable is globally available again.</span></strong><span> Last week (Wed, 1 July), Anthropic’s leading model, Fable, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c016ce37-d610-4462-a38b-7f004322725c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>became</span></a><span> available to all after Anthropic resolved its differences with the US Government, which had banned foreign nationals from using it. Wired </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c99f6887-5130-4321-aa2b-f6584587b463?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reported</span></a><span> that a few days prior, Anthropic stopped CEO Dario Amodei from talking with the White House, and cofounder Tom Brown took over communication with the administration. Whatever changed, it clearly worked.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fable is a very capable model based on my experience, and feels “smarter” than previous ones. But personally, I’m at the point of struggling to figure out </span><em><span>how much </span></em><span>better a new model is than an older one. Testing leading models against each other is one way to go, so let’s talk about GPT-5.6.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>GPT-5.6 is OpenAI’s latest model, released today</span></strong><span> (Thursday, 9 July). A select group of individuals and companies have had access to the model, and shared their impressions:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenCode creator Dax Raad:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 I guess the proof will be “in the pudding.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Gaining the trust of developers takes years, not a single release, and Meta has burnt through developers’ trust over the last decade. </span></strong><span>To be a serious coding model contender, Meta would need to offer cheaper </span><em><span>or</span></em><span> better models than the state-of-the-art. They already did it cheaper, which is a start! But Meta will need to keep this up for </span><em><span>years</span></em><span> if they are to regain developer trust.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I recall how the company burnt developers in 2016, when the company abruptly shut down Parse without offering any migration path, after buying the beloved “backend-as-a-service” for mobile apps in 2013. Any software engineer building on Parse learnt an important lesson: do NOT use Meta’s services for anything important, no matter how good the pricing is!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building Muse Spark 1.1 model evidently took a major toll on Meta’s engineering organization, with employees forced into model training, unnecessary layoffs, and morale plummeting, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/178c718e-b779-4344-87a6-334bafdd1bb1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>we covered extensively</span></a><span>. It’s good that all this effort was not for nothing, but I have doubts on whether Meta can keep competing with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Cursor, longer term. They all have access to far more professional coders as users, and therefore have more feedback loops for improving coding models. Those companies have also gained the trust of millions of software engineers, already.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Where is Gemini?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s surprising is that Gemini is no longer a top-three coding model.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Google has invested massively in AI to take on OpenAI and Anthropic, but Gemini does not have a model comparable in performance to Fable, GPT-5.6 or Grok 4.5. In the middle: Nikodem, who was an AI faker, using an AI mask.</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unfortunately for the candidate, Ilya was born in Russia and his stepfather is Polish, so he can recognize a Polish accent – or lack thereof. During the interview, he became suspicious and asked: “can I stop you for a second, why do you have a Korean accent?” Two seconds later, “Nikola” disconnected, suggesting strongly that an AI faker had been exposed. Ilya suspects such impersonators will soon be deploying deepfake voices to be even harder to detect:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I know the difference between a Polish and a Korean accent... But this isn’t the case for a lot of people. This person used a deepfake face, but soon enough they’ll have a deepfake accent. Please be vigilant.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the full exchange captured on video </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c2d1dee6-4040-42ab-b3b3-69ade61b9b94?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in Ilya’s LinkedIn post.</span></a><span> Sadly, North Korean agents attempting to get hired under fake identities is nothing new: we shared this trend happening a year back, in the deepdive </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c463dbc9-944d-4b81-9408-346e0249e7e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>AI fakers exposed in tech dev recruitment: postmortem.</span></a></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Oops.. Meta’s key logging exposed sensitive data</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Devs at Meta have been extremely unhappy to have all their keystrokes logged and screens recorded to help train Meta’s AI, and things got worse when Meta managed to leak sensitive data internally. On the upside, the social media has now stopped its controversial data gathering exercise, reports </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/148ef631-7788-4c16-8898-debbfeaa1ef1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>WIRED</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Meta left potentially sensitive information collected from employee laptops accessible to anyone inside the company, according to an internal security notice seen by WIRED and three current employees familiar with the issue.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The data, which was collected as part of a divisive initiative to train artificial intelligence models, is believed to include keystrokes, mouseclicks, and content displayed on the computer screens of Meta’s US employees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton initially confirmed to WIRED that the company is investigating the security issue. As this story was being published, he added that Meta is pausing the data collection program indefinitely.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This reads to me like a sloppy implementation of an internal tool, reminiscent of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa4838a2-91bc-4e97-aa4e-63178b36eea4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft’s security fiasco with Recall</span></a><span>. In fairness, Microsoft’s was more embarrassing because it was customer data that could be easily accessed. For Meta, this is “just” internally-recorded sensitive information that could be accessed by some insiders.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Massive cuts at Xbox</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Xbox is letting go about 20% of staff in a sudden, deep layoff round. New Xbox CEO Asha Sharma </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d33a473-da03-4d3a-8bc3-59c873d6ae6f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> cutting 3,200 people from a workforce of ~16,000, with 1,600 being let go immediately, and the rest throughout next year. To her credit, she did not blame AI for these cuts and explained the business problem Xbox has:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Xbox margins are 3-10x lower than competitors</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The latest generation of Xbox consoles have a smaller install base and higher cost structure than Playstation 5</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The Game Pass bet (pay $10-23/month for access to 36-500+ games) has not worked out</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Microsoft bought a bunch of independent game studios, but is managing them at a loss</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Asha is implying the business has been mis-managed and is now greatly underperforming versus Sony’s Playstation business, and so big changes are needed. To illustrate how big some of these changes will be, the layoff includes Kevin LaChapelle, a veteran with a 37-year long Microsoft tenure (!!)</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" loyalty to a large tech company is rarely returned, no matter how long the tenure, or someone’s contributions. On the positive side, I assume that Kevin, and other long-tenured employees were offered a generous severance.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Meta can’t buy enough AI capacity from Google</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two weeks ago, when covering how Meta is destroying its engineering organization in pursuit of a leading coding model, I expressed confusion about why Mark Zuckerberg has decided that building a coding LLM is more important than keeping Meta’s core business running smoothly. Last week, there may have been an answer. The Financial Times </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eccb2b9c-b925-47b4-8f74-7aecee2e1721?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reports</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Google has put limits on Meta’s use of its Gemini AI models after the social media giant sought more computing capacity than the rival tech group could provide, in the latest evidence of the infrastructure constraints facing even the world’s largest AI providers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Google told Meta around March that it could not provide all of the Gemini capacity the company wanted to purchase, according to three people familiar with the matter, in a move that has disrupted and delayed some of Meta’s internal AI projects.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta not being able to buy enough tokens for its own AI sounds like a good enough reason to want to build its own model! And now they have: Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 is a more capable model – based on benchmarks they released – than anything that Google has to offer.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Qualcomm acquires Modular</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Chris Lattner is creator of vLLM and Swift, and cofounder of Modular, which made the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4589546d-af69-4c0f-9a6d-ea69bdc968f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Mojo</span></a><span> programming language. In somewhat surprising news, Chris’s company has been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ea10ecb-087f-457b-8e95-c6c990a26864?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>acquired by</span></a><span> chip maker, Qualcomm.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The acquisition presumably makes a lot of financial sense for Modular, otherwise it’s hard to imagine why they would sell to a hardware vendor. Mojo’s selling point was that it avoids vendor lock-in when programming CPUs and GPUs. But as Qualcomm is a chip vendor, it could be tricky for GPU vendors like NVIDIA and AMD to embrace this language. Or perhaps I am wrong, and Qualcomm is not seen as much of a threat by GPU vendors like NVIDIA.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Commenting on the acquisition, Modular CEO Lattner said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The acquisition by Qualcomm enables us to accelerate our mission without deviating from supporting hardware from all vendors. This will accelerate our progress and path, and their vision is expansive: spanning edge to cloud, CPU, GPU, NPU, and custom ASICs and perhaps more.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What is certain is that with Qualcomm buying it, Modular does not have to worry about raising the next round of funding, and the team can focus heads-down on Mojo and inference. My sense is that Lattner does his best work when he can focus on building, and he’ll surely have the opportunity to do this inside Qualcomm, as he did back at Apple.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yes, I’d prefer a vendor-neutral language and platform like Mojo succeed, and hopefully this will still happen. Of course, congrats to the Modular team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>We previously did a podcast episode </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ae5182f9-6109-451b-a43d-7b2db426616d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with Chris Lattner on LLVM, Swift and Mojo.</span></a></em></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Memory price hikes hit Apple products</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Every system that processes data eventually has to answer one question. When is the data complete enough to be moved to the compute stage?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A program adding up a day’s sales needs to know whether all of today’s sales have actually arrived. For data stored in a file, the answer is trivial because the file has an end. However, for data that arrives continuously and never stops, there is no clean answer, and how a system resolves that gap is the difference between batch processing and streaming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Batch processing waits for completeness. It collects data up to a natural boundary, a closing time, or a finished file, and then computes over the whole set at once. Streaming prioritizes completeness for speed. It produces answers continuously from data that is still arriving, which means it has to estimate when enough data has come in and handle the cases where that estimate is wrong. This trade-off between completeness and latency is the key consideration when dealing with streaming and batch.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size:
