You can also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f210a54f-0f23-478f-9863-66c0676f8662?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>check out Antithesis.</span></a></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this special “ask me anything” episode of Pragmatic Engineer podcast, I am in the hot seat facing questions sent in by subscribers that are read out by guest Volodymyr Giginiak, CTO and cofounder of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/751eeea8-9acd-4973-a1ed-12523ae3ede6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Wordsmith AI</span></a><span>, a legal tech startup </span><em><span>(note: I’m </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/20e7fa9f-0077-4a1b-8ac6-c34c2b5278e4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>an investor</span></a><span>)</span></em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I tackle your questions on the software industry, AI, hiring, engineering organizations, career growth, the business model of the Pragmatic Engineer, and more. We also discuss where software engineering is headed, and I offer advice on some specific situations. </span><em><span>Thanks to everyone who sent questions!</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>Three stories & observations</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/da085ff9-8590-4044-9034-f7a9fdfd91f3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/cSIMVYjVF28" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Story #1: Without the COVID-19 pandemic, The Pragmatic Engineer might not exist. </span></strong><span>Prior to the global health crisis in 2020, I had no plans to get serious about writing: I enjoyed blogging on The Pragmatic Engineer blog, but intended to remain an engineering manager or software engineer for the foreseeable future.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then, COVID-19 happened and Uber made layoffs, which led to a quarter of my team being let go, while the rest of us were disbanded into other teams. It was a tough time, and I decided it was a good moment to exit and finish writing a book I had been working on, ‘The Software Engineer’s Guidebook’. After that project was complete, I planned to try and start a VC-funded startup and build something around platform engineering; possibly a system for tracking RFCs at mid-sized and larger companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I gave myself around eight months to finish the book, but when that deadline elapsed, it still wasn’t ready. I did write three other books (‘The Tech Resume Inside-Out’, ‘Building Mobile Apps at Scale’, and ‘Growing as a Mobile Engineer’) and still wasn’t convinced by any startup idea. But I did discover that I like to write!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Story #2: I was on track to publish a damning exposé, until one message from an engineer changed my mind.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During the first year of The Pragmatic Engineer, I wrote about conditions for engineers at the Dutch neobank Bunq, based on accounts from disgruntled employees. I had a final draft ready, which I sent to the company to provide a right of reply ahead of publication. Then I received a message.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was sent by an engineer originally from the Middle East. They told me they had really wanted to break into the European tech industry, but that no company would sponsor their visa, except Bunq. Yes, the company was a tough place to work at as a dev – and this engineer subsequently left for another opportunity – but they appreciated Bunq for taking a chance on them that enabled them to move to Amsterdam and learn how to build fintech with a small team. This engineer now works at Meta and attributes their success to the break Bunq provided.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on that interaction, I opted not to publish the article, and it also led me to adopt a new editorial policy that I have followed since: I write about what </span><em><span>works </span></em><span>inside companies, instead of focusing on what </span><em><span>seems</span></em><span> to be broken.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Story #3: Being called a “nobody” by a CEO led to my </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/64a82b3d-043e-42fe-9afa-8c40ed088c4e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>sole investigative piece</span></a><span>, which uncovered some pretty interesting details. </span></strong><span>After I briefly noted Pollen’s poorly-handled layoffs, CEO Callum-Negus Fancey dismissed my report during a company all-hands, and compared The Pragmatic Engineer unfavorably to the BBC as just some minor publication with an agenda against Pollen (why I would have an anti-Pollen bias isn’t clear to me!) To be honest, I took it personally when I heard a recording of this sent to me by employees there, and so started digging around.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I discovered unpaid salaries, silently cancelled health insurance in the US, and the CTO deliberately triggering a $3.2M double charge to customers and never publishing a postmortem, despite engineers requesting one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was certainly something, and I published the findings in the article </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/64a82b3d-043e-42fe-9afa-8c40ed088c4e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Inside Pollen’s Collapse: “$200M Raised” but Staff Unpaid - Exclusive</span></a><span>. To ensure the CEO saw the report on a platform he deemed worthy, I also contributed to the BBC’s documentary: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad37ff29-22f3-4824-9d72-1ad52352c683?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Crashed: $800M Festival Fail</span></a><span>, aired in the UK during prime time. By doing all this, I also learned that investigative journalism is just not for me.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a strange turn of events, someone at Pollen evidently </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b1b0498d-caf3-4280-9f7a-c0136012725a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wants my original article to disappear from Google’s search results</span></a><span>, and filed bogus DMCA takedown notices a few weeks ago. Well, it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b1b0498d-caf3-4280-9f7a-c0136012725a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>having the opposite effect!</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Opinion #1: I believe LeetCode-style interviews will stay because they self-select tolerance of corporate nonsense. </span></strong><span>The existence of data structures and algorithm (DSA) interviews is a bit of a head scratcher because these skills are rarely used at work. However, a candidate who’s willing to grind for weeks or months to prepare for an interview which bears little resemblance to the job, is likely to be someone who understands that sometimes it’s necessary to do pointless work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This suggests they’ll probably have a much better time in Big Tech than someone who refuses to engage with meaningless tasks. It’s one reason I’ve observed for companies retaining LeetCode-style interviews. Of course, AI solves the puzzles with ease these days, and I expect larger companies to move back to in-person interviewing – all while keeping DSA interview questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Opinion #2: MCP became industry standard partly because Anthropic wasn’t a threat – but it couldn’t pull this off today. </span></strong><span>When MCP </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/87d2f8ee-0245-4d7b-ba7e-1b98cdc339c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>launched</span></a><span> in November 2024, Anthropic wasn’t yet considered </span><em><span>the</span></em><span> leading AI lab. GPT-4o was seen as the top-performing multimodal model, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro. At that point, Claude 3.5 Sonnet was seen as the best</span><em><span> coding </span></em><span>model, but it wasn’t understood how advantageous being good at coding would be for AI in general.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and other players could adopt MCP without fear of lock-in, as it came from a promising, but not a dominant lab. When Google launched its </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5369c2ca-234a-4c49-adbc-4a84fa119866?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Agent2Agent protocol</span></a><span> a few months later, no major lab adopted it due to concerns about Google’s dominant position. Today, Anthropic is </span><em><span>the</span></em><span> leading frontier lab and I reckon this would discourage adoption if MCP was launched in the present climate, for the same reason as nobody adopted the Agent2Agent protocol.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My answer to subscribers with questions about how to create standards is that I see them as emerging somewhat coincidentally, following a technically strong approach and with the right external conditions in place, which are impossible to entirely predict or control.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Opinion #3: My hot AI take: AI doesn’t make work easier, and be mindful of skill atrophy</span></strong><span>. If you’re using AI and life seems to be getting a lot easier, it raises the question: are you trying hard </span><em><span>enough</span></em><span>? Personally, using AI forces me to think just as hard, or even harder than before. I choose to use zero AI in my writing for the Pragmatic Engineer, and Grammarly is turned off as well. This is because I don’t want my writing skill to degrade, and would like to keep improving. On the other hand, with coding, I do use AI and accept my hand-coding ability will unavoidably degrade. My tip is to be mindful of the tradeoffs inherent in AI, and to keep using those skills which you value and want to keep sharp, even when AI tools are available.</span></p><h3 justify"><span>PR-AF is an open-source code review agent that ranks #2 of 42 on Martian's Code-Review-Bench, ahead of CodeRabbit, Copilot, and Devin, running a single open model. The trick is the harness: it plans a review strategy per PR, spawns parallel reviewer agents, verifies every finding against your source, and drops anything it cannot prove. That makes it about 10x cheaper per review than closed-source tools. One API call, and a drop-in GitHub Action. If open models writing frontier-level reviews sounds useful, star the repo.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Agentfield_070826","text":"Fork and deploy!","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e52abda-3d99-4b1c-a83e-8ec208a76907?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Fork and deploy!</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A chatbot answers a question, and an agent completes a task. This seems like a huge difference. However, the gap between the two is narrower than it appears.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An agent is an LLM placed inside a loop where the model itself decides when the loop should stop. Everything interesting about agents follows from this shift. The autonomy that makes them useful, the cost that makes them expensive, and the design challenges that come with building one all trace back to it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It helps to see where that shift sits in the broader picture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Software built around language models has moved through a recognizable progression. It started with a single LLM call that took an input and produced an output. Then, the function calling arrived, which let the model reach out to a tool when it needed information or wanted to take an action. After that, developers began chaining calls together in code, with each step’s output feeding into the next, to handle problems too large for a single call. The most recent of these is the agent, where the developer hands control of the loop itself to the model and lets it iterate until it decides the work is done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will walk through that progression. We will also look at how an agent is structured, what choices the model makes on every turn, what scaffolding holds it together, and when an agent is actually the right pattern to reach for.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Foundations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Before the loop can be interesting, the unit that sits inside it has to be clear.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A bare large language model call is a stateless function. Text goes in, text comes out, and each call typically stands alone in the model’s view. If we want it to fetch today’s weather or update a record in a database, the bare model lacks the means to do either. It can describe weather in general terms and talk about how a database record would change, but reaching the actual forecast or touching the actual database requires something more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>What makes the model useful in real systems is augmentation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In other words, we give it the ability to call functions we have defined, often called tool use or function calling. We give it access to a retrieval layer that can pull in relevant documents at runtime. We also give it a way to write down information that it should carry between calls, which acts as memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Anthropic calls the combination of these capabilities the augmented LLM, and treats it as the foundational unit of every agentic system. The augmented LLM is the building block from which everything else gets composed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the unit most developers have already worked with, even if they have called it something else. Examples include a chat assistant that runs Python code, a function-calling API wired to your service, and a RAG application that pulls from your documents. These systems are useful, and they are also still one call. The model produces an output, the system returns it, and the interaction ends until the next request arrives.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Workflows</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>What happens when a problem reaches beyond what a single call can handle?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The natural response is to string calls together in a sequence we design, a pattern called prompt chaining. Each step in the chain is its own LLM call, and the output of one step becomes the input to the next. We might use one call to draft an outline, a second call to expand the outline into paragraphs, and a third call to translate the paragraphs into another language. The chain is fixed in advance, and the developer writes which steps run, in what order, and what each step’s prompt looks like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the family of patterns Anthropic groups together as workflows.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A workflow is a system where the LLM and its tools are orchestrated through a code path that the developer designed. Beyond prompt chaining, there are other workflow patterns:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Routing classifies the input and sends it to a specialized handler.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Parallelization runs subtasks at the same time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Orchestrator-worker has a manager LLM that delegates pieces to specialist LLMs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Evaluator-optimizer has one call to generate while another critiques, with the cycle iterating until quality is good enough.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The details differ, but every workflow shares the same property. The number of steps and the path through them are decided by the developer at design time, before the model sees the input. Most production systems built on LLMs today are workflows. They are predictable, debuggable, and usually cheaper than full-blown agents.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Loop</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An agent is what we get when we wrap an LLM in a loop and let the model decide when the loop should exit. The loop itself is plain code. The runtime calls the LLM, reads the output, dispatches whatever action that output specified, feeds the result back into the model’s view, and calls the model again. This continues until the model produces a response that signals a final answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There are four steps inside each iteration, and we can call them perceive, reason, act, and observe:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Perceive is the moment the loop hands the model the current state, which includes the original task, the history of what has happened so far, and any new input.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Reason is the model’s turn, where the model produces a response that says what to do next, whether that means asking a question, calling a tool, or wrapping up with a final answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Act is when the runtime carries out whatever the model asked for.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Observe is when the result of that action gets captured and folded back into the state, so the model sees it on the next perceive step.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most important detail is who decides when the loop should stop. In a workflow, the developer decides at design time how many steps run. In an agent, the model decides at runtime. The model exits the loop by producing an output that the runtime interprets as a final answer. The developer typically sets a hard ceiling on the number of iterations, often called a max-turns parameter, but that ceiling is mainly a safety net. The primary stop signal comes from the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Observation matters as a first-class step for the same reason.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The model needs to see the result of its actions before deciding the next move. Removing observation would collapse the loop into a chain, with the model running on prior expectations rather than fresh results from the world. The closed loop, where every action is followed by an observation, is what lets the model adjust as it goes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>With the loop established, the next question is what actually happens on each turn through it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Decisions</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>On every turn through the loop, the model’s output picks one of four branches, and the runtime acts on that pick. This branching makes the loop feel intelligent because the LLM is choosing what kind of move to make. Here are the four branches:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Final answer:</span></strong><span> The model produces what amounts to a complete reply to the original task. The runtime interprets this as the loop’s exit signal, returns the result, and stops.</span></p></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Tool call:</span></strong><span> The model produces an instruction asking the runtime to invoke a specific function with specific arguments. The runtime executes the tool, captures whatever it returned, appends that result to the conversation state, and sends control back to the model so the loop continues.</span></p></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Handoff:</span></strong><span> The model decides that the current task belongs in the hands of a different agent, often a specialist with its own prompt and tool set. The runtime swaps which agent is running and feeds the same state into the new agent, with the loop continuing under the new identity.</span></p></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Continued thought:</span></strong><span> The model produces a reasoning turn that consists of thought alone. The runtime captures the thought, feeds it back into the state, and runs the model again. This branch shows up most often in ReAct-style implementation, which we are about to see.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>OpenAI’s Agents SDK documents the first three branches as first-class behaviors of its loop. The fourth is more a property of how a particular prompt is written than a separate code path</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>ReAct</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>ReAct is the prompting pattern that stands for Reasoning plus Acting. The pattern asks the model to interleave reasoning steps with action steps inside the same response, so the model can think about what to do, do it, see what happened, and adjust.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A ReAct trace reads like a structured journal. The model produces a thought, then an action, then receives an observation from the runtime, then produces another thought, and so on, until it reaches a final answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Imagine an agent handling customer support:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A user asks for the status of their most recent order.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model produces a thought first, reasoning that it needs to find that order and that the order service is the right place to look.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It then takes an action by calling the get_recent_order function with the user’s ID.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The runtime executes the call and feeds back an observation telling the model that the order is number 9152, placed on May 14.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model produces another thought, working out that it now needs the shipping status for that specific order.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It calls the get_shipping_status function with the order ID. The observation comes back, saying the order is in transit and expected to arrive on May 29.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model has what it needs at this point and produces a final answer summarizing the status for the user.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" justify"><span>Two things to consider from this flow are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>First, every action is grounded in an observation, which is the closed-loop point from the previous section made concrete.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Second, the reasoning steps are doing real work, since they are how the model decides which action makes sense next, given what it has learned so far.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>ReAct is one way to fill the loop, and it is by far the most common pattern in the agent frameworks we work with today.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Guardrails</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Guardrails belong at the points where the loop crosses into the outside world. They are part of the architecture itself, designed in alongside the loop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For reference, OpenAI’s Agents SDK documents three families of guardrails, all defined by where in the loop they run.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Input guardrails run on the first turn, before the agent’s main model sees anything. They are the place to catch things like prompt injection attempts, requests that violate policy, or inputs that fall outside the agent’s scope. A common pattern is to use a small, fast model as the guardrail, so the more expensive main model only runs when the input passes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Tool guardrails wrap every function-tool invocation. A tool input guardrail runs before the tool executes and can block the call or replace it with a message back to the model. A tool output guardrail runs after the tool executes and can rewrite or block the result before it goes back into the conversation state. Tool guardrails matter because tools are how the loop touches systems we care about, and that touch needs supervision.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Output guardrails run on the final response, after the loop has decided to terminate, but before the user sees the result. They are the last layer of policy enforcement and the place to catch things like leaked sensitive data or claims the agent should avoid making on the company’s behalf.</span></p></li></ul><div justify"><span>The structural point is that guardrails sit at every interface where the loop meets the world.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Handing control of the loop to a model is powerful, and it comes with three costs that every developer should understand before using the pattern:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Compounding error:</span></strong><span> Per-step reliability does poorly when steps are chained together, and the math is not favorable. If the model succeeds on each step of a loop 95 percent of the time, the joint probability of every step going right across ten steps is roughly 60 percent. Stretch that to twenty steps, and the joint success rate falls to about 36 percent. The autonomous nature of agents brings higher costs and potential for compounding errors. The reason coding agents work better than open-ended task agents is that test feedback raises per-step reliability, which shortens the effective length of the chain that has to succeed.</span></p></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Scaffolding around the loop:</span></strong><span> The harness around the loop matters as much as the model inside it. For example, Anthropic shared an internal experiment where even a frontier model running in the Claude Agent SDK fell short on building a production-quality web app from a high-level prompt. The fix was scaffolding rather than a better model. They built an initializer agent that lays out a feature list before any feature work starts, a coding agent that picks one feature per session, a progress file that travels between sessions, and a git history that the agents can use to recover.</span></p></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>The wrong tool for the job:</span></strong><span> An agent is often the wrong choice. It is important to find the simplest solution and only add complexity when needed, which sometimes means avoiding agentic systems entirely. Workflows offer predictability and consistency. Agents offer flexibility, and they pay for that flexibility in latency, money, and a more unpredictable failure surface. Many problems are served better by a chain.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The agent loop sits at the end of a recognizable progression.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We started with a single LLM call that takes text in and returns text. We added tools, retrieval, and memory to get the augmented LLM. We strung calls together into workflows when one call was outgrown. The agent is the next rung, the point where the developer hands the control flow itself to the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Inside the loop, four steps repeat. The model perceives the current state, reasons about it, takes an action, and observes the result. On every turn, the model’s output picks one of four branches. These are a final answer, a tool call, a handoff, and a continued thought. ReAct is the most common prompting pattern for filling the loop, with reasoning and action interleaved. Guardrails live at every place where the loop crosses into the outside world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The design carries three real costs. These are compounding reliability across steps, the harness scaffolding that production loops require, and the question of whether a workflow would solve the problem more cheaply.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>What is the tech jobs market like for job seekers and hiring managers today? It’s a broad question for which one answer is that it’s a land of contrasts and confusion, and also some crossed wires. Experienced engineers and managers feel ghosted by employers and recruiters, who in turn have given up on inbound applications because their inboxes are full of AI slop, sometimes from bogus candidates. It’s rosier for those with </span><em><span>specific</span></em><span> skillsets, who are in strong demand – and personal networks help more than ever to land the right job.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For this final part of our series on the tech hiring market during the first half of 2026, I spoke with more than 50 hiring managers, software engineers, and engineering leaders. </span><em><span>Thank you to everyone who contributed!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For more on this topic, check out our analysis of what the data says about the market in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/655fa96e-2b26-4f4b-bfd0-e8510d87055c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Part 1</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a14312a4-0299-45c7-bc0a-0d416c4c3313?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Part 2</span></a><span> of this mini-series.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Overall, an appropriate description of the employment market as many folks experience it right now would be “weird”. This is a characteristic that’s not easy to see in the data, but is clear from talking to people and hearing their anecdotal, personal accounts of job hunting this year. I think the data in the first two articles of this series failed to capture just how unusual things are.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>So, in today’s issue, we attempt to shed some light on the weirdness, covering:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Catch-22:” nobody finds each other. </span></strong><span>Hiring managers struggle to find experienced folks, who barely get any replies when applying for jobs. How’s that work?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No trust. Is AI to blame? </span></strong><span>AI-enhanced resumes read as incredible, but hiring managers often face disappointment. Some places don’t bother reading inbound applications as a result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Hot market for some, but tough for most</span></strong><span>. For those in AI Engineering, ML, or </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f7d6755c-a053-41db-8fe8-b647bdc70545?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>FDE</span></a><span>, the market is incredible. For everyone else, it’s much less great.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Higher hiring bar & lower compensation – but not for everyone. </span></strong><span>Many candidates are unhappy with offers that are the lowest in years. This doesn’t apply to AI Engineering positions or at AI businesses, however.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering leader recruitment: also weird for senior ICs.</span></strong><span> Senior engineering leaders are struggling to find opportunities, or may turn them down in favor of fractional roles or to work on their own startup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>US market trends. </span></strong><span>Folks experiencing the “best market ever” are likely in the US, where a talent shortage is a bigger complaint than it is elsewhere.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Trends in the UK, EU, and rest of the world. </span></strong><span>“Ghosting” is more commonplace than in the US, “fake applicants” a bigger issue, remote roles are going extinct, and more.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. “Catch-22:” nobody finds each other</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The phrase “Catch 22” refers to a paradoxical problem, whose solution is blocked by the problem itself. The term originated in a famous World War II novel of the same name, and it also describes pretty accurately what I see in today’s tech job market. Hiring managers are saying that highly-skilled talent (typically senior+ engineers) is not available to be recruited, at the same time as experienced, proven professionals find their applications ignored by employers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What seems paradoxical here is how both can be true. It’s as if recruiters and potential candidates aren’t hearing each other. Of course, there’s some nuance:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table take</span></a><span> on the hiring market</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mike Julian, CEO of DuckBill Group, which is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d368f7f-33d9-41ec-bc1c-b13371095d9d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: underline;"><span>observation</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>“We get about 1,000 applications a day on inbound and maybe two of them are even relevant to the posting.</span><br><br><span>I mostly no longer look at inbound seriously because it’s so c***. I’d almost certainly miss a great inbound submission if it came in.</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All of our recent hires have been via network and us reaching out to folk on LinkedIn. Biggest hurdle we have to outreach is thin LinkedIn profiles and little other online presence.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">From the other hiring managers we talked with, more themes emerged:</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>More inbounds than ever & also more noise</span></h3><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>I’ve never seen so many inbounds and strong resumes.</span></strong><span> I’m hiring for lots of roles; for one software engineering position in Seattle, we have had 800 resumes inbound over a three-month period. I’ve never seen anything like this! These resumes are not low-quality either: they are people who have worked at MSFT, AWS, other large tech companies, and have solid skills.”</span><em><span> – Head of Engineering, Series B startup, Seattle, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s difficult to find good candidates among all the noise. Have had two open senior engineer positions for months, and the only good interviews or offers we’ve extended were in network.” </span><em><span>– Engineering Manager, late-stage startup, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>A glut of vastly underqualified people completely drowning your hiring pipeline. </span></strong><span>This is what I’m seeing, and it’s making inbound a useless channel.”</span><em><span> – Engineering Director, Big Tech, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“From what I hear from recruiters, every job posted has 1,000+ applicants, and 98% of them are considered unqualified.”</span><em><span> – fullstack engineer, Middle East</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“We are a small company and gave up on inbound hiring. </span></strong><span>We got too many AI applications. Much lower signal-to-noise compared to past experience.”</span><em><span> – Director of Engineering, Canada</span></em></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Experienced engineers struggle to get interviews</span></h3><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Even when you’re good, it feels like there’s a LOT of noise to cut through to get noticed.</span></strong><span> I’m quietly looking for a new role in devtools, and fit that ‘product engineer’ profile perfectly. I feel like the demand for great people is higher than ever, but I can’t figure out where on that bar I fall.”</span><em><span><span> – Tech lead, seed-stage startup, US</span><br></span></em><span><br><span>“As an experienced engineer & successful-ish founder I have yet to get to a phone screening in this job market. There is clearly something amiss, just a wall of noise preventing any signal from getting through.”</span></span><em><span> – Software engineer + founder, 8 years experience, US</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A staff engineer at a late-stage startup in the US summed things up:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It feels like everyone who has a good job is holding onto it for dear life, and THOSE are the people we want to hire.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>“Tale of two cities:” in demand or not</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A director of engineering at a Big Tech in the US, identifies two distinct groups in the market:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>If you are at the top of your game, have AI experience, and are senior enough, you can write your own ticket</span></strong><span>. If not, then the job market is tough! This job market is like the tale of these two very different cities.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Observations from some job seekers echo this: demand feels strong for “AI-adjacent” engineers (those building AI systems), especially in the US. Standout engineers with a strong network are still in demand, and we covered the story of one such person in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e33b9b89-667b-4c40-939c-67c3314d4dd5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>“How to be a 10x engineer” – interview with a standout dev</span></a><span>. For everyone else, it’s a struggle to get an interview!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Referrals: more important than ever?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Several experienced engineers currently on the job market say they only get interviews when they personally know someone at a company:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Larger companies have to have some serious AI going on to sift through resumes because they are being bombarded. It really is the case that you don’t get your resume seen unless you know people who can vouch for you.”</span><em><span> – Technical Program Manager, Big Tech, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>Referrals are a lifeline. </span></strong><span>It’s impossible to get interviews for Staff or Principal Eng positions by cold applying. The only interviews I am getting from a cold-apply are Senior-level roles.” </span><em><span>– Principal Engineer, 10 YOE, US</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From a couple of hiring managers:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The only interviews or offers we’ve extended were to devs already in our network.” – </span><em><span>Software architect at a mid-sized company, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I filled an engineering manager position in record time thanks to a person in my network looking for this job. If it would not have been for my network I would probably have been looking for someone for a couple of months.”</span><em><span> – VP of Engineering, private equity-funded company, Germany</span></em></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. No trust. Is AI to blame?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hiring managers repeatedly tell us they no longer trust what they read in resumes, and that some candidates even turn out to be fake.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Polished CVs, weak candidates</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common gripe among hiring managers is that resumes are highly optimized by AI, but candidates turn out not to have the experience they claim:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>CVs are high-quality, but the people behind them are not. </span></strong><span>Almost every resume looks impressive. However, the quality of the conversations does not match it at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One recent example: I interviewed a senior candidate who had spent five years at a US-based cloud consulting company, most recently as an architect. I asked which architectural principles or patterns he had used in his projects. His answer was: “Daily standup, sprint planning, and retrospective.” I clarified that I meant from a tech perspective, not process perspective. He confidently replied: “Yes, daily standup, sprint planning, and retrospective.” </span><em><span>– Engineering manager, large company, Berlin, Germany</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Ten years ago, we would have appreciated resumes tailored to a role that was posted, now it’s just lazily thrown together with AI.”</span><em><span> – Engineering Manager, mid-sized company, Canada</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AI-keyword stuffing is rampant</span></strong><span>, according to one head of engineering in the UK:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Lots of people are rebranding themselves as senior AI Engineers and demanding much higher salaries. Their resumes now have lots of AI-related keywords mentioned, like RAG, evals, inference… but when digging deeper there is little substance. Many of them are seeking a senior level salary (£90k–£140k) when they are barely showcasing mid-level skills.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Cover letters are as good as dead,</span></strong><span> several hiring managers tell us. The reason is that they’re always AI-generated, boring to read, and pointless. </span><em><span>More than 18 months ago, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c42a44d6-9c49-4a65-bd75-098d391957ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>we reported on</span></a><span> how cover letters were being made redundant by AI in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac87f6d4-0840-4b6d-9686-1d1ef9e1fd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>How GenAI is reshaping tech hiring.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An engineering manager at a UK e-commerce agency summarizes what’s happening:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“’Claude; write me a CV that matches this job spec, then auto send’. This seems like the name of the game for most applicants.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Fake candidates</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Does anything encapsulate the challenges of today’s job market for recruiters more succinctly than candidates who do </span><em><span>not</span></em><span> exist, even when they appear to be sitting in an interview? A year ago, we covered an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10cd3c61-d196-4823-8c1c-fb223a3afddd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>“AI faker” applicant caught by a security startup</span></a><span>, who was potentially a state agent from North Korea.</span></p><div In extreme cases, the interviews are being outsourced so that a different person shows up for the interview. It feels a bit like playing captcha with them during interviews.”</span><em><span> – Senior EM, private-equity backed company, Bay Area, US</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“The second person we interviewed was clearly a North Korean scammer, writing questions into an LLM, reading the response, easily tripped up, and other interviews were background noise in the room.”</span><em><span> – Staff Engineer, UK</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Many applicants that looked a good fit turned out to be someone else in the Asia Pacific region doing interviews with an AI in the background. It’s easy to spot because of the ‘lag’ in a naturally flowing conversation.”</span><em><span> – head of engineering, mid-sized company, Germany</span></em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cheating in remote interviews by using AI is also commonplace. A software engineer based in Finland told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A couple of times we saw an applicant who was using AI to answer the questions, and this was sooo weird. I honestly didn’t know how to react, so we decided to cut the interview short. We then shared a note with the recruiters on how to spot this.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Hot market for some, but tough for most</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The market appears sharply bifurcated: amazing for AI and a few specialist roles, and a major struggle for everyone else.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Some accounts from folks benefitting in the current conditions:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“The market is really good as an (AI) engineer with the right experience. </span></strong><span>I’m not actively looking but get 2–3 messages a day. When I was hiring for AI engineers at my last AI startup, the market for these folks was terrible. It’s very hard to find good talent, and people that were great on paper did poorly in interviews.”</span><em><span> – AI Engineer, 5 YOE, New York, US</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It seems like demand for senior positions is still there, but only if your profile really matches what the company needs. For example, I’ve been working on different data pipelines for a while, and finding such a position is relatively simple. However, breaking into anything else is not! Every startup wants to hire only people experienced in that particular thing they need.”</span><em><span> – Software Engineer, 13 YOE, Big Tech, UK</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s what two job seekers who are struggling at present say:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“I sent my handcrafted resume to 30–40 positions, and heard back from zero.</span></strong><span> Eventually, I got an interview after a recruiter reached out via LinkedIn; I don’t know how I would’ve found anything, if it was not for this!”</span><em><span> – Software engineer, 5 YOE, Amsterdam, Netherlands</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As a developer without a specific “specialization,” I’m struggling to get any interviews. I’ve spent a few years as frontend, then another few as backend, and most recently working on DevEx. In this market, I just don’t get any callbacks for interviews, not even a first round interview.”</span><em><span> – Software engineer, 6 YOE, London, UK</span></em></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple
